items.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years attends his annual review. An early-morning urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 5.2 mg/mmol; eGFR is 81 mL/min/1.73m².
items.explanation: A raised uACR (above 2.5 mg/mmol in men) can be transient, for example after exercise, fever or a UTI. Kidney Health Australia and the RACGP advise confirming albuminuria with 2 of 3 raised samples within 3 months before diagnosing diabetic kidney disease. Once it is confirmed, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is titrated and an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured.
why: An ultrasound is for unexplained or progressive CKD, haematuria or suspected obstruction, not for confirming early albuminuria with a normal eGFR.
A timed 24-hour collection is awkward and less reliable than repeat spot uACR, and no longer advised for screening or confirmation.
Electrophoresis looks for a paraprotein (myeloma), which is not suggested by isolated albuminuria in long-standing diabetes.
A biopsy is kept for atypical features such as rapid eGFR decline, active sediment or no retinopathy, not for unconfirmed moderate albuminuria.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with small cell lung cancer becomes drowsy. She is clinically euvolaemic, BP 130/80 mmHg. Sodium 117 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 540 mOsm/kg.
items.explanation: Her serum is hypotonic but her urine is inappropriately concentrated, she is euvolaemic and her potassium is normal. This pattern is SIADH, and ectopic ADH secretion by small cell lung cancer is its classic cause in palliative care. Management is fluid restriction, then specialist options such as urea or tolvaptan, and sodium should be corrected slowly.
why: Primary adrenal insufficiency would usually cause high potassium and low blood pressure, but her potassium and BP are normal.
Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia needs clinical signs of volume loss, and she is euvolaemic.
In primary polydipsia the urine is maximally dilute (below 100 mOsm/kg), not concentrated.
Cerebral salt wasting follows brain injury and causes hypovolaemia, which does not fit this euvolaemic patient.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is sweaty and disoriented in the emergency department. He refuses treatment for a foot abscess and demands to leave.
items.explanation: Decision-making capacity can only be judged fairly once reversible causes of impairment are excluded. In an insulin-treated patient who is sweaty and disoriented, hypoglycaemia is the most likely and fastest-reversible cause, and a bedside glucose check takes seconds. If he is hypoglycaemic, correcting it may restore his capacity, and his decision about treatment can then be reassessed.
why: Hyponatraemia can cause confusion, but it does not explain sweating in an insulin-treated diabetic, and the result takes longer than a bedside glucose.
Imaging is not the first step when no head injury or focal signs are described and a reversible metabolic cause is far more likely.
Intoxication is possible, but sweating with disorientation in a person with type 1 diabetes points first to hypoglycaemia, which must be excluded urgently.
A cognitive screen does not assess capacity for a specific decision and is meaningless until an acute reversible cause like hypoglycaemia is ruled out.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man is struck on the chin by a cricket ball. He has malocclusion and a step in his lower teeth. An orthopantomogram shows a displaced left parasymphyseal fracture.
items.ask: Which other fracture is most likely?
items.explanation: The mandible behaves like a ring, so it usually breaks in two places. A blow to one side of the chin that causes a parasymphyseal fracture often also fractures the condylar neck on the opposite side. Check the orthopantomogram for this second fracture, and look for pre-auricular tenderness on that side.
why: The zygomatic arch is part of the midface, and a blow to the chin does not pass force up to it.
Force from a parasymphyseal impact travels to the condyle on the opposite side, not the condyle on the same side.
Orbital floor blowout fractures come from a direct blow to the orbit, not to the chin.
Nasal fractures need a direct blow to the nose and are not linked to mandibular ring fractures.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman, not breastfeeding, has a red retroareolar lump unresolved after five days of flucloxacillin. Ultrasound shows an abscess and a separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins.
items.ask: Most appropriate next step for the mass?
items.explanation: The collection is the abscess, but the separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins looks malignant and an abscess cannot explain it. In a non-lactational infection that has not responded to antibiotics, this mass needs a tissue diagnosis, and core biopsy is the preferred method to complete triple assessment.

Waiting for the infection to settle gives false reassurance and delays the diagnosis of a mass that already looks malignant.

MRI does not give a tissue diagnosis, and tissue is what this suspicious mass needs next.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl is on the paediatric ward of a regional hospital, 6 hours after treatment began for severe diabetic ketoacidosis at the first presentation of type 1 diabetes. At presentation she weighed 40 kg. Her venous pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 3 mmol/L, glucose 41.0 mmol/L, sodium 130 mmol/L and urea 14.2 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, then fluids to replace her deficit over 48 hours with added potassium. An insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour was started after the first hour. She now has a severe headache, has vomited once, and is irritable and disorientated. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 64/min (previously 128/min), blood pressure 134/86 mm Hg (previously 106/64 mm Hg), respirations 20/min and SpO2 98% on room air. Her GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6). Her pupils are equal and reactive. Capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L and serum sodium is 134 mmol/L.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT brain before any further treatment
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour
Increase the fluid rate to replace the deficit over 24 hours
Intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes
items.explanation: This girl has cerebral oedema, the main cause of death in children with DKA. She has several risk factors: a first presentation, young age, severe acidosis and a high urea at presentation. It typically appears 4 to 12 hours into treatment. The warning signs are a new headache, vomiting, irritability or confusion, a falling GCS, and a falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (part of the Cushing response). The RCH DKA guideline and ISPAD 2022 say to treat on clinical grounds straight away. Give IV mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes, or 3% hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes. At the same time, cut the fluid rate by one third, raise the head of the bed, call senior and intensive care help, and arrange retrieval or transfer. Imaging comes only after she is stable. CT brain should not delay treatment, because a normal early scan does not rule out cerebral oedema and she could herniate while waiting for it. Bicarbonate is itself linked to cerebral oedema and has no role here. Faster fluids would make the brain swelling worse. Her glucose of 15.8 mmol/L rules out hypoglycaemia as the cause of her confusion.
why: Wrong: imaging must not delay treatment, because cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically and an early CT may be normal; scan only once she is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is linked to cerebral oedema and is not indicated; her acidosis is improving with insulin and fluids.
Wrong: giving fluid faster makes cerebral oedema worse; the fluid rate should be cut by one third, not increased.
Wrong: her capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L, so hypoglycaemia does not explain her confusion, and the change in her heart rate and blood pressure points to raised intracranial pressure.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man who drinks heavily every day is brought in confused and unsteady. He has horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based gait. Capillary glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Confusion, nystagmus and ataxia in a heavy drinker point to Wernicke encephalopathy. The next step is urgent high-dose parenteral thiamine (eTG: 500 mg IV three times daily), given before any glucose. It should be started on clinical suspicion, without waiting for tests.
why: Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in people with alcohol use disorder and cannot reach therapeutic levels quickly enough for Wernicke encephalopathy.
His glucose is normal, and giving glucose before thiamine can make Wernicke encephalopathy worse.
He has no tremor, sweating or tachycardia to suggest alcohol withdrawal, and a benzodiazepine does not treat thiamine deficiency.
With no head injury or focal signs, imaging would only delay time-critical thiamine, which should come first.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation comes to the maternity assessment unit because her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 38 weeks, and that infant was small for gestational age. In this pregnancy she has diet-controlled gestational diabetes. A scan at 32 weeks showed an estimated weight on the 40th centile. She takes low-dose aspirin. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min and temperature is 36.7 °C. Symphysis-fundal height is 35 cm. A urine dipstick shows no protein. A 40-minute cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a baseline rate of 135 bpm, baseline variability of 10 bpm, three accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds, and no decelerations. She feels several movements during the trace.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day sonographic biometry and liquor volume assessment
Discharge with routine antenatal review at 37 weeks
Continuation of the CTG for a further 40 minutes
items.explanation: Every feature of this CTG is normal by RANZCOG criteria: the baseline is 110 to 160 bpm, variability is 6 to 25 bpm, there are accelerations and there are no decelerations. Her observations and urinalysis show no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. A normal CTG means the fetus is not hypoxic right now. It does not rule out underlying placental insufficiency or growth restriction, so it does not exclude a later poor outcome. The Stillbirth CRE guideline on decreased fetal movements says that when a woman has risk factors for growth restriction or stillbirth, she should have an ultrasound for fetal biometry and amniotic fluid volume, ideally within 24 hours, along with obstetric review. This woman has a previous small-for-gestational-age stillbirth and gestational diabetes. The scan should be arranged today. She should then be told to come back straight away, at any hour, if movements decrease again.
why: Sending her home with routine follow-up treats the normal CTG as if it rules out compromise, which is unsafe in a woman with risk factors for stillbirth.
A single episode of reduced movements with a normal CTG and a normal assessment is not a reason for birth at 35 weeks, and preterm induction brings neonatal risks with no proven benefit.
The trace already meets every normal criterion with a good signal, so recording for longer adds no information about her placental reserve.
A Kleihauer-Betke test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage, which would be suspected with a sinusoidal or abnormal trace, trauma or bleeding, and none of these is present here.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has mild scleral icterus after gastroenteritis with poor oral intake. Bilirubin is 42 µmol/L (unconjugated 38 µmol/L); ALT, ALP, full blood count and reticulocytes are normal.
items.explanation: His bilirubin is mildly raised and almost all unconjugated. Liver enzymes are normal and there is no sign of haemolysis, and it came on during fasting and illness, so this is Gilbert syndrome. It is benign and needs only reassurance, not further investigation.
why: Haemolysis would raise the reticulocyte count and usually lower the haemoglobin, but his full blood count and reticulocytes are normal.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome raises conjugated bilirubin, not unconjugated bilirubin.
Acute viral hepatitis would raise ALT sharply and cause a mixed or conjugated rise in bilirubin.
Biliary obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and ALP, and his ALP is normal.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD and a 50 pack-year smoking history has five months of worsening breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows a large right pleural effusion. NT-proBNP is 160 ng/L.
items.ask: This result argues most against which cause?
items.explanation: An NT-proBNP below 300 ng/L makes heart failure very unlikely, whatever the patient's age. Heart failure also usually causes bilateral transudates, so a large one-sided effusion with a normal NT-proBNP points away from a cardiac cause and towards malignancy.
why: NT-proBNP does not reflect tumour burden, so a normal level does nothing to rule out lung cancer in this heavy smoker.
Mesothelioma is a pleural tumour that does not raise NT-proBNP, so a normal level does not argue against it.
A parapneumonic effusion is judged by fever, white cell count, CRP and pleural fluid pH, not by NT-proBNP.
A tuberculous effusion is judged by exposure history, a lymphocytic exudate and fluid AFB and culture, which a normal NT-proBNP does not affect.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed car crash, breathless with BP 82/50 mmHg. Her trachea deviates left and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.
items.explanation: She has a right tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock. This is diagnosed on clinical signs and needs immediate decompression, by needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line or by finger thoracostomy. An intercostal catheter on an underwater seal follows.

A hyper-resonant chest points to trapped air rather than haemothorax, and fluid will not relieve obstructive shock.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has left-sided ulcerative colitis confirmed on colonoscopy. Symptoms began 3 months ago. Liver function tests are normal. She asks about bowel cancer risk.
items.explanation: Colorectal cancer risk in ulcerative colitis goes up with how long the disease has lasted and how much of the colon is involved. Australian guidelines (Cancer Council Australia, GESA) advise a first surveillance colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. The interval after that depends on her risk, for example whether she has PSC, active inflammation, strictures or a family history.

Waiting 15 years would miss the period when dysplasia and cancer risk are already rising.
Age 45 is the starting age for average-risk population screening, and it does not apply to colitis-related risk.
Age 50 is an older population screening age that ignores how long she has had colitis, so cancer could be found late.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man who smokes has had a painless, indurated ulcer on the lateral tongue for 5 weeks, persisting after an adjacent sharp tooth was smoothed.
items.explanation: An indurated oral ulcer that has not healed after 3 weeks, even once the possible cause of trauma is removed, is treated as squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. The diagnosis is made on tissue. An incisional biopsy taken from the edge of the lesion gives the histology and is the definitive test, ideally performed after urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery or head and neck surgery.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents in labour at 39 weeks' gestation. An endocervical NAAT taken two days ago is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and she has not been treated.
items.ask: Which neonatal complication is most likely?
items.explanation: The baby can catch gonorrhoea during a vaginal birth. The main risk is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, a heavy pus-filled conjunctivitis that usually starts 2 to 5 days after birth and can quickly damage the cornea. To prevent it, treat the mother and give the exposed newborn a single dose of ceftriaxone, as eTG and RCH advise.
why: Afebrile pneumonitis at 4 to 12 weeks is typical of chlamydia caught at birth, not gonorrhoea.
Chorioretinitis is a feature of congenital toxoplasmosis or CMV, not gonococcal infection.
Sensorineural hearing loss is the classic long-term result of congenital CMV.
Snuffles (syphilitic rhinitis) is caused by congenital Treponema pallidum infection, not gonorrhoea.

items.stem: A 71-year-old retired plumber, exposed to asbestos, has three months of right shoulder pain and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a 5 cm right apical mass.
items.ask: Which complication is he most at risk of?
items.explanation: A right apical mass with shoulder pain points to a superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour. These tumours invade nearby structures: the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1) and the cervical sympathetic chain. Damage to the sympathetic chain on the same side causes Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), so you should examine his eyes and hands.
why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch and is affected by left hilar or mediastinal disease, not a right apical mass.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome mainly linked to small cell lung cancer, and it does not come from local invasion.
A right-sided tumour would affect the right phrenic nerve, and the phrenic nerve runs medially, not through the superior sulcus.
Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration is rare and mainly linked to small cell lung cancer, so it is much less likely than local invasion.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with confusion and petechiae. Platelets are 18 x 10^9/L and haemoglobin is 82 g/L; the blood film shows schistocytes. Coagulation studies are normal.
items.explanation: Low platelets, haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes on the film, neurological signs and normal coagulation point to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which is a medical emergency. Urgent plasma exchange, usually given with corticosteroids, should start without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result, because untreated TTP is often fatal.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man is hypotensive (BP 78/50 mmHg) with a rising central venous pressure six hours after coronary bypass grafting. His mediastinal drain output has suddenly stopped after heavy bleeding.
items.explanation: Low blood pressure and a rising CVP after heavy bleeding that suddenly stops draining point to cardiac tamponade from clotted blood after cardiac surgery. The definitive treatment is emergency resternotomy, done at the bedside if the patient is crashing, to remove the clot and control the bleeding.
why: After cardiac surgery the tamponade is usually clotted and loculated, so a needle often cannot drain it and the bleeding is left uncontrolled.
A vasopressor does not relieve the mechanical blockage to cardiac filling and only delays definitive treatment.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man ran a petrol generator inside a closed shed and was found unconscious. After oxygen therapy he is now alert with normal neurological examination and carboxyhaemoglobin 4%.
items.ask: Which complication is he most at risk of?
items.explanation: After significant carbon monoxide poisoning, especially with loss of consciousness, delayed neurological sequelae can appear days to weeks after apparent recovery. They include memory loss, cognitive and personality change, and parkinsonism. He should be counselled about these symptoms and arranged neurocognitive follow-up, even though he is well at discharge.
why: Pulmonary fibrosis follows paraquat or chronic dust exposure, not carbon monoxide poisoning.
Peripheral neuropathy is a feature of chronic lead, arsenic or solvent exposure, not a typical result of acute carbon monoxide poisoning.
Posterior subcapsular cataracts are linked to radiation, corticosteroids or electrical injury, not to carbon monoxide.
Acute kidney injury can occur from rhabdomyolysis during the event, but chronic kidney disease is not the expected long-term risk in a patient who has recovered.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has two days of sharp chest pain eased by sitting forward, following a cold. ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; troponin is normal. Ibuprofen is started.
items.ask: Which added drug most reduces recurrence?
items.explanation: Recurrence is the commonest complication of acute pericarditis and happens in up to about 30% of patients. Under eTG and the 2025 ESC guidelines, colchicine for 3 months is added to an NSAID: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg, or twice daily from 70 kg. It roughly halves the recurrence rate and speeds symptom relief.
why: Corticosteroids are not first-line, and early use in viral or idiopathic pericarditis actually raises the risk of recurrence.
Hydroxychloroquine is used for lupus serositis, which has not been shown here, and it does not prevent recurrence of viral or idiopathic pericarditis.
Beta-blockers may ease the tachycardia, but they do nothing to the pericardial inflammation or the recurrence risk.
A proton pump inhibitor is given as gastroprotection with the NSAID, but it does not change the risk of recurrence.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer on regular oral morphine has two days of drowsiness and multifocal myoclonus. Creatinine is 240 µmol/L (baseline 80 µmol/L); corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L.
items.explanation: The creatinine has risen sharply from baseline, which means acute kidney injury. The kidneys clear morphine's active metabolites (morphine-3- and morphine-6-glucuronide), so these build up and cause drowsiness and myoclonus. Management is to reduce or stop the morphine and switch to an opioid less affected by kidney function, such as fentanyl or hydromorphone, while treating the cause of the kidney injury.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man sees his general practitioner with a 1-day history of a painful, swollen left knee. He cannot bear weight. Two days ago he knelt on a rusty nail while clearing soil in his garden shed and did not clean the small wound. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and osteoarthritis of both knees. His record shows he completed his childhood primary immunisation course, and his last booster was given 12 years ago after a hand laceration. He has no allergies and no immunosuppressive conditions or medicines. His temperature is 38.7 °C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 134/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. There is a 2-mm puncture wound stained with soil below the left patella. The knee is hot, with a large effusion and pain on any passive movement. Capillary glucose is 13.8 mmol/L. Same-day hospital transfer for joint aspiration has been arranged.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional preventive measure at this visit?
options: Serum tetanus antitoxin level before vaccinating
items.explanation: The main issue in this man is septic arthritis from direct inoculation, and he has already been referred for aspiration before antibiotics. A separate risk that is easy to miss is tetanus. A puncture wound from a rusty nail, contaminated with soil and left untreated for more than 6 hours, is tetanus-prone. Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, a person with a documented primary course of 3 or more doses and a tetanus-prone wound needs a tetanus-containing vaccine if it has been 5 years or more since the last dose. In Australia this is usually dTpa. His last booster was 12 years ago, so he needs one injection now. Tetanus immunoglobulin is for people with fewer than 3 doses, an uncertain history, or significant immunocompromise. Well-managed type 2 diabetes on metformin does not count as significant immunocompromise for this purpose. Giving the booster now, at the first visit, means it will not be missed during the hospital admission.
why: Wrong: tetanus immunoglobulin is only added when the primary course is incomplete or uncertain, or the patient is significantly immunocompromised, and none of these applies to him.
Wrong: immunoglobulin on its own gives only short-lived passive protection and does not boost his immunity, which has waned since his last dose 12 years ago.
Wrong: a full primary course is only for people who are unvaccinated or have an uncertain history, and his record shows a completed childhood course.
Wrong: antitoxin levels are not used to guide wound management, and waiting for the result would delay a booster he clearly needs now.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has central chest tightness, now settled with GTN. BP 136/80 mmHg. ECG shows new lateral ST depression; hs-troponin T rises from 40 to 115 ng/L.
items.explanation: She has a high-risk NSTEMI: no ST elevation, but dynamic ST depression and a rising troponin above the 99th percentile. Her pain has settled and she is haemodynamically stable, so the very-high-risk 2-hour pathway does not apply.

items.stem:
A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting about 400 mL of bright red blood at home. He has passed black stools for 2 days. He has drunk about 10 standard drinks of beer daily for 20 years, and his last drink was last night. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented. He has spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. The abdomen has shifting dullness, and the spleen tip is palpable. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and a crystalloid bolus is started. Laboratory studies show:
Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180)
Platelets 74 x10^9/L (150–400)
INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2)
Urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.5)
Creatinine 90 µmol/L (60–110)
Albumin 26 g/L (35–50)
The gastroenterology registrar plans endoscopy within the next few hours.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
Pantoprazole infusion as the only drug therapy
Red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L
items.explanation: This man has an upper GI bleed with features of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets, a raised INR and a low albumin. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure point to significant blood loss. The bleed should be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and Baveno VII, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours, or octreotide) should start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy. It lowers portal pressure, improves control of bleeding and reduces mortality. Patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding should also get antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). This reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and death. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and the extra volume can raise portal pressure. A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does nothing for a variceal bleed and would delay vasoactive therapy and antibiotics. Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding. Balloon tamponade is wrong at this stage because it is a temporary bridge for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy.
why: Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis, eTG advises against routinely correcting it, and the extra volume raises portal pressure.
A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does not lower portal pressure or treat a variceal bleed, and it leaves out the vasoactive drug and antibiotics the guidelines require.
Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding.
Balloon tamponade is wrong because it is only a temporary rescue for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy, and endoscopy is already planned.

The left temporal artery is thickened, tender and pulseless. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left. items.stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed in the coronary care unit 3 hours after emergency coronary angiography. She came to the emergency department with central chest pain, fever and a productive cough 2 days after her sister's funeral. Her ECG showed ST elevation in V2 to V4. Angiography showed no obstructive coronary disease, and left ventriculography showed apical ballooning. Her chest X-ray shows right lower lobe pneumonia, and she is receiving ceftriaxone and azithromycin. She has had 1 L of crystalloid since arrival. Temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on 2 L/min oxygen. She has a new harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her JVP is not raised, and there are crackles at the right base only. Bedside echocardiography shows an LVEF of 35%, apical akinesis with hyperdynamic basal segments, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a peak left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 70 mmHg. Serum lactate is 2.9 mmol/L (reference below 2.0).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing her low blood pressure?
items.explanation: This woman has Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: two stress triggers (her sister's death and pneumonia with sepsis), apical ballooning, and no culprit lesion on angiography. She now has one of its most dangerous complications, dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. The basal segments contract too hard, which pulls the anterior mitral leaflet into the outflow tract (systolic anterior motion, SAM). That causes the new systolic murmur, a gradient of 70 mmHg and hypotension. The obstruction gets worse with anything that empties the ventricle or makes it contract harder: low preload, low afterload, tachycardia or inotropes. Her JVP is not raised, she has no pulmonary oedema, and sepsis has left her relatively low on fluid, so the first step is a cautious crystalloid bolus to fill the LV and widen the outflow tract. Reassess after each bolus. If hypotension persists, the next options are a pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine, a short-acting beta-blocker if she can tolerate it, or mechanical support that does not lower afterload. Inotropes are avoided. This is the key safety point after Takotsubo is diagnosed in a shocked patient: get an echo to look for an LVOT gradient before giving any inotrope.
why: Wrong: dobutamine is an inotrope that makes the basal segments contract harder and speeds the heart, which worsens SAM, raises the LVOT gradient and can deepen the shock.
Wrong: a nitrate dilates veins and arteries, lowering preload and afterload, which narrows the outflow tract, worsens the obstruction and would drop her blood pressure further.
Wrong: a diuretic lowers preload in a woman with no pulmonary oedema and a JVP that is not raised, so the LV cavity shrinks and the obstruction gets worse.
Wrong: a balloon pump lowers afterload, which can increase the LVOT gradient, so it is not recommended in Takotsubo with outflow obstruction.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of fever and constant, diffuse abdominal pain. Over the past 3 weeks his abdominal girth has increased. Alcohol-related cirrhosis was diagnosed 3 years ago. He has not attended follow-up and drinks about 10 standard drinks daily. He has never had abdominal surgery and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 38.4°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. He is jaundiced. His abdomen is distended, with shifting dullness and mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding or rigidity. Serum results: albumin 24 g/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, LDH 190 U/L (reference less than 250 U/L) and creatinine 124 µmol/L. A diagnostic paracentesis under ultrasound guidance yields cloudy, straw-coloured fluid. Fluid results: white cell count 2100 x10^6/L with 75% neutrophils, total protein 8 g/L, albumin 5 g/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L and LDH 105 U/L. The Gram stain shows neutrophils and no organisms.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the paracentesis results?
options: High-gradient ascites with infection and no Runyon criteria for a surgical source
Low-gradient ascites with infection suggesting tuberculous peritonitis
High-gradient ascites with infection meeting Runyon criteria for perforation
High-gradient ascites with a polymorph count below the threshold for infection
Low-gradient ascites with infection suggesting peritoneal carcinomatosis
items.explanation: Read the fluid in three steps. First, the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is 24 − 5 = 19 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more means the ascites is due to portal hypertension, which fits his cirrhosis. Second, the absolute neutrophil count is 2100 x 0.75 = 1575 x10^6/L. Anything at or above 250 x10^6/L confirms ascitic infection, so IV antibiotics and IV albumin should start without waiting for the culture. Third, look for a surgical source using the Runyon criteria: protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L, or LDH above the serum upper limit. His protein is 8 g/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L and LDH 105 U/L, so he meets none of them. The Gram stain shows no organisms, and he has no peritonism. Together these point to spontaneous rather than secondary bacterial peritonitis. The low protein (below 10 g/L) is also a risk factor for SBP, and he will need long-term prophylaxis after this episode.

Wrong: secondary peritonitis needs at least two Runyon criteria, and his protein (8 g/L), glucose (5.6 mmol/L) and LDH (105 U/L, below the serum limit) meet none, with no organisms on Gram stain.
Wrong: the absolute neutrophil count is 1575 x10^6/L, far above the diagnostic threshold of 250 x10^6/L, so this misreads the 75% as the count or ignores the threshold.
Wrong: peritoneal carcinomatosis gives a low gradient and high protein, whereas this fluid has a gradient of 19 g/L and protein of 8 g/L, which point to portal hypertension.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward on the morning he is due to go home. He takes no other medicines. Today his temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft and not tender. items.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the fetal medicine clinic at 17 weeks pregnant to discuss her amniocentesis result. She conceived naturally. At 10 weeks, whole-genome cell-free DNA screening (fetal fraction 11%) showed a low chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and of sex chromosome conditions, and a high chance of trisomy 16. A 7-week scan had shown one gestational sac. The 12-week scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks, with QF-PCR and chromosomal microarray, showed a normal female result with no trisomy 16. Both of her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She has no medical history, does not smoke, and takes folic acid and iodine. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Ultrasound today shows a single live fetus with biometry consistent with dates, no anomaly seen, normal amniotic fluid and a high posterior placenta. She is blood group O RhD positive, and her antibody screen is negative.

items.explanation: The screening result was valid (adequate fetal fraction) and showed a high chance of trisomy 16, but amniocentesis found a chromosomally normal fetus. The vanishing twin explanation is unlikely because she conceived naturally and an early scan showed one sac. The most likely explanation is therefore confined placental mosaicism (CPM): the trisomic cells are in the placenta, which supplies most of the cell-free DNA. RANZCOG/HGSA (C-Obs 59) and ISPD advise amniocentesis rather than CVS for rare autosomal trisomies for exactly this reason, because the placenta itself is likely to be abnormal. CPM involving chromosome 16 is strongly linked with placental dysfunction, which raises the risk of intrauterine growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. A normal amniocentesis result means the fetus is reassuring, but the pregnancy is still high risk. She needs continued care with a fetal medicine or obstetric team, serial growth and Doppler scans in the second half of pregnancy, blood pressure monitoring, and counselling to report reduced fetal movements. Many units also consider low-dose aspirin.

After amniocentesis, leaking of fluid is uncommon and usually happens within days, so a procedure done a week ago with normal fluid today adds little later risk.
Placental dysfunction from trisomy 16 mosaicism tends to reduce amniotic fluid rather than increase it, and no fetal anomaly or diabetes is present to cause polyhydramnios.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of headaches for 7 weeks. They began when she started working 12-hour shifts at a desk to meet the end-of-financial-year deadline at her accounting firm. Before this she had only occasional mild headaches. The headache is a bilateral, band-like tightness that builds through the afternoon. She rates it 4/10. It now comes on every afternoon. She has no nausea or photophobia, and climbing stairs does not make it worse. She takes paracetamol 1 g about five times a week and ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week, which takes the edge off it. She drinks four standard drinks a week and does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Her trapezius and temporalis muscles are tender. Passive neck flexion is full and painless. Fundoscopy shows sharp discs with venous pulsations, and the neurological examination is normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to prevent progression of her headache disorder?
options: Switch to paracetamol with codeine on headache days
Take ibuprofen 400 mg regularly three times a day
Start amitriptyline 10 mg each night as prevention
Use sumatriptan 50 mg at the onset of each attack
Limit acute pain relief to fewer than 10 days per month
items.explanation: This woman has tension-type headache: it is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate and not made worse by activity, she has no nausea or photophobia, her pericranial muscles are tender, and it started with a clear trigger (long hours at a desk under deadline stress). Her examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. The main risk for her is medication-overuse headache. She is already taking simple analgesics on about 25 to 35 days in every 4 weeks. ICHD-3 defines medication-overuse headache as headache on 15 or more days a month with regular overuse for more than 3 months. The threshold is 15 or more days a month for simple analgesics, and 10 or more days a month for triptans, opioids or combination analgesics. At 7 weeks she has not met the time criterion yet, but she is well over the frequency threshold. Following eTG, she should keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (roughly 2 to 3 days a week), keep a headache diary, and avoid codeine. Treatment should be mainly non-drug: posture and ergonomics, regular breaks, sleep, exercise, physiotherapy and stress management.
why: Codeine-containing combination products cause medication-overuse headache at a lower threshold (10 or more days a month), cause dependence, and eTG advises avoiding opioids in tension-type headache.
Taking ibuprofen regularly every day guarantees analgesic overuse, which raises her risk of medication-overuse headache as well as gastrointestinal and kidney harm.
Preventive amitriptyline is kept for established chronic tension-type headache that has not responded to non-drug measures, and it does nothing about her current analgesic overuse.
Triptans do not work for tension-type headache and cause medication-overuse headache at only 10 or more days a month, so taking one with every daily attack would make things worse.

items.stem: On the paediatric ward, a 3-year-old boy recovers after bronchoscopic removal of a peanut that caused chronic cough and left-sided wheeze. His parents ask how to protect him and his 14-month-old sister.
items.explanation: Inhaled foreign bodies are most common between 1 and 3 years of age, and nuts are the classic culprit. Australian advice (RCH, Kidsafe) is to give no whole nuts or similar hard, small foods to children under 5 years, and to supervise them seated at meals. Nut allergy prevention still uses smooth nut pastes, not whole nuts.
why: ASCIA advises introducing peanut early as smooth paste to prevent allergy, and delaying it adds allergy risk without reducing choking risk.
Puréeing everything is not needed and holds back feeding development; the aim is to avoid hard, small, round foods.
ANZCOR advises encouraging a child who is coughing effectively to keep coughing, and back blows are only for an ineffective cough.
Once the object is removed and the child recovers, routine serial X-rays do not prevent another inhalation.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who drives a delivery van has had a first unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. CT brain and electrolytes are normal. He asks that his employer not be told.
items.explanation: The biggest risk after a seizure is a crash that harms him and the public. Under the Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive standards, he must stop driving and tell the licensing authority himself, and a commercial driver faces a longer stand-down. You keep his confidence with his employer. If he keeps driving anyway, you may notify the authority, and in some states you must.
why: Sleep deprivation is a sensible trigger to avoid, but it matters much less than the risk of a crash.
Not swimming alone is reasonable safety advice, but it mainly protects him, and the danger to the public from driving comes first.
His employer has no right to his health information without his consent, and keeping him safe on the road is handled through the licensing authority.
Medicine is not usually started after one unprovoked seizure with normal tests, and it would never be lifelong from the start.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman is drowsy in recovery 2 hours after hysteroscopy and curettage. Curettings contained fat; she has peritonism and BP 90/55 mmHg after 1 L crystalloid. Laparotomy is arranged.
items.ask: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Fat in the curettings means the uterus has been perforated and bowel may be injured, so she needs treatment for peritonitis, not just surgical prophylaxis. eTG recommends IV amoxicillin (or ampicillin), gentamicin and metronidazole, which together cover enteric Gram-negative bacilli, enterococci and anaerobes, started alongside resuscitation and urgent laparotomy.
why: A single prophylactic dose of cefazolin does not cover anaerobes or enterococci, so it is not enough treatment for peritonitis from a possible bowel injury.
Vancomycin with gentamicin gives no anaerobic cover and targets MRSA, which is not the likely pathogen from a bowel perforation.
An oral drug is wrong for a shocked patient going to theatre who is nil by mouth and needs reliable IV dosing.
This is a PID and STI-type regimen; azithromycin adds nothing for bowel flora and leaves enterococci uncovered.

items.stem:
A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a 1-day history of worsening headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. For 5 days before this he had right ear pain. He has no medical history, takes no medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respirations 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. He has neck stiffness, no rash, sharp optic discs and no focal neurological deficit. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Blood cultures are taken and a lumbar puncture is done. Ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg are given straight after the procedure. Results:
Blood: leucocytes 19.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 185 mg/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L
CSF: turbid; opening pressure 28 cmH2O; white cells 1900 x10^6/L (90% polymorphs); red cells 6 x10^6/L; protein 2.1 g/L (0.15 to 0.45); glucose 1.2 mmol/L; Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
items.explanation: The CSF is turbid, with many polymorphs, a high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 1.2/6.0 = 0.2 (below 0.4), so this is bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the probable source is his right acute otitis media. Some pneumococci have reduced susceptibility to penicillin and ceftriaxone. So eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone as soon as Gram-positive diplococci are seen, and continuing both until susceptibility results are back. Treatment is then narrowed to suit the organism. Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days, because it gives the most benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. Amoxicillin covers Listeria and is added only for patients at risk: those over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or with alcohol dependence. He has none of these risks, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus. Aciclovir is not needed: he has no confusion, seizures or focal signs, and the CSF picture is clearly bacterial with organisms seen. Changing to benzylpenicillin before susceptibility is known risks undertreating a resistant strain.
why: Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which shows as Gram-positive bacilli and is a risk only in people over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or alcohol-dependent, and he is none of these.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, but he has no encephalitic features and the CSF is clearly bacterial, with organisms seen.
Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days in pneumococcal meningitis because this is the organism where it most reduces death and hearing loss.
Narrowing to benzylpenicillin is done only after susceptibility testing confirms a sensitive strain, so changing now could undertreat a resistant pneumococcus.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital 3 hours after central chest pressure began. The pain spreads to his left arm, and he has sweating and nausea. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He drinks about 4 standard drinks per week and has had no falls, injections or strenuous exercise. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 150/92 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is not raised, the chest is clear, and there is no hepatomegaly or peripheral oedema. An ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. A chest X-ray shows clear lungs. Blood taken from a newly inserted cannula shows: potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2); bilirubin 10 µmol/L (<20); ALT 28 U/L (<45); AST 71 U/L (<35); ALP 80 U/L (30–110); GGT 30 U/L (<50); creatine kinase 590 U/L (<200); hs-troponin T 210 ng/L (<14).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's aspartate aminotransferase (AST) result?
options: In vitro haemolysis of the blood sample
items.explanation: The AST is raised on its own. ALT, bilirubin, ALP and GGT are all normal, and this happens alongside an anterior STEMI, a raised creatine kinase and an hs-troponin T well above the 99th percentile. AST is found in cardiac muscle as well as in liver and skeletal muscle. It leaks from infarcting myocardium, which is why it was once used as a cardiac marker. ALT is much more specific to the liver, so a normal ALT with a normal cholestatic profile points away from liver disease. Here the AST is best read as part of the myocardial infarction. It does not need liver work-up, and it must not delay reperfusion. Troponin, not AST, is the marker to follow for myocardial injury.
why: Wrong: an AST:ALT ratio above 2 can suggest alcohol, but he drinks very little, and his GGT and ALT are normal.
Wrong: congestive hepatopathy needs raised right-sided pressures, but his JVP is normal, there is no hepatomegaly or oedema, his lungs are clear, and ALT and bilirubin would usually rise too.
Wrong: in vitro haemolysis would also raise the potassium, which is normal at 4.1 mmol/L, and the sample came from a fresh cannula.
Wrong: he has had no trauma, falls, injections or exertion, and the raised troponin with ST elevation places the enzyme source in the heart, not skeletal muscle.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man who smokes has 4 weeks of constant left forefoot pain at night, eased by dangling the leg. His second toe is dry and black; left ABI is 0.32.
items.explanation: This is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: he has had ischaemic rest pain for more than 2 weeks, has dry gangrene and an ABI below 0.4. The limb is at high risk of amputation, so he needs to be discussed with the vascular team the same day, with a view to imaging and revascularisation. Meanwhile, give analgesia, keep the leg dependent, protect the foot and start an antiplatelet and a statin.
why: Supervised exercise is used for intermittent claudication, but he now has rest pain and tissue loss, so exercise therapy is not appropriate and would delay revascularisation.
The gangrene is dry and shows no signs of infection, such as redness, pus or fever, so antibiotics do not treat the underlying ischaemia.
A routine outpatient referral is too slow for a threatened limb with established tissue loss, and the delay risks a major amputation.
Cilostazol only improves walking distance in claudication; it does not save a limb with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and should not replace urgent referral.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man develops headache and nausea after running a petrol generator in a closed garage. He is alert, with a normal neurological examination. Carboxyhaemoglobin is 18%.
items.explanation: This is mild to moderate carbon monoxide poisoning with no neurological features. The treatment is 100% oxygen through a non-rebreather mask as soon as possible, which shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin from about 5 hours to about 1 hour. Continue it until he has no symptoms and his carboxyhaemoglobin is below about 3–5%. Hyperbaric oxygen is only discussed with a hyperbaric unit for severe cases.
why: Hyperbaric oxygen is considered only for severe poisoning, such as loss of consciousness, neurological deficit, cardiac ischaemia or pregnancy, and this patient has none of these.
Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide poisoning, as in smoke inhalation with high lactate, and does nothing for carbon monoxide.
Low-flow nasal oxygen gives too little oxygen to speed up carbon monoxide removal much, and a normal pulse oximetry reading here gives false reassurance.
Methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia, such as from nitrites or dapsone, and does not treat carboxyhaemoglobinaemia.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with heart failure on furosemide and perindopril took naproxen for a week; now breathless and oedematous. BP 152/88 mmHg, warm peripheries. Creatinine 151 µmol/L (baseline 92).
items.ask: Most likely cause of his AKI?
items.explanation: He is taking a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor, and adding an NSAID makes the "triple whammy". The NSAID blocks the prostaglandins that widen the vessel into the glomerulus, while the ACE inhibitor stops the vessel out of it from tightening, so filtration falls and the creatinine rises. The same drug also makes him hold onto salt and water, which explains why his heart failure got worse, so stopping the NSAID is a key part of treatment.
why: Low-output cardiorenal syndrome needs poor perfusion, but his BP is 152/88 mmHg and his peripheries are warm.
He is fluid overloaded, not dry, so volume depletion does not explain the creatinine rise.
Nothing in the case points to urinary retention, and a recent NSAID gives a clearer explanation.
Renal artery stenosis shows up as a creatinine rise when an ACE inhibitor is started, not during a stable long-term course after an NSAID.

items.stem:
A 73-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a dry cough that has been getting worse for 4 months. He also has breathlessness when walking uphill, a hoarse voice and a constant dull ache below his right clavicle. He has lost 5 kg without trying. He is a retired electrician who worked around asbestos lagging in the 1970s, and he has never smoked. He takes perindopril for hypertension. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The right apex is dull to percussion. He has no clubbing, lymphadenopathy or conjunctival pallor. A chest X-ray shows a 5 cm rounded opacity at the right lung apex. Blood results are:
Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130 to 180)
MCV 87 fL (80 to 100)
White cell count 8.1 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150 to 400)
Bilirubin 11 µmol/L (less than 20)
Creatinine 95 µmol/L (60 to 110); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2
Corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60)
ALP 98 U/L (30 to 110)
Albumin 32 g/L (35 to 50)
CRP 18 mg/L (less than 5)
items.ask: Which of the following best explains the abnormalities in these blood results?
options: Bone marrow infiltration by metastatic tumour
Erythropoietin deficiency from chronic kidney disease
Anaemia of inflammation due to an underlying malignancy
Haemolysis from a paraneoplastic autoimmune process
Vitamin B12 deficiency from poor dietary intake
items.explanation:
The bloods show a mild anaemia with a normal MCV (normocytic), a mildly raised platelet count, a mildly raised CRP and a low albumin. In an older man with weight loss and a 5 cm apical mass that is lung cancer until proven otherwise, this pattern fits anaemia of inflammation (anaemia of chronic disease). Tumour-driven cytokines such as IL-6 raise hepcidin, which traps iron and suppresses red cell production. The same cytokines cause a reactive thrombocytosis, a raised CRP and a low albumin. In lung cancer, thrombocytosis and hypoalbuminaemia also point to a worse prognosis.

The normal results matter too. The corrected calcium is normal, so there is no hypercalcaemia (from PTHrP or bone metastases). The normal ALP and bilirubin give no blood evidence of bone or liver spread, although normal bloods do not rule out metastases. Renal function is adequate for contrast CT. None of these results changes the plan: he still needs an urgent CT of the chest and upper abdomen and urgent referral to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team, with the aim of being seen within 2 weeks (Cancer Australia; Optimal care pathway for lung cancer).

Why the other options are wrong:
B: Marrow infiltration usually lowers the counts or gives a leucoerythroblastic film, often with a raised ALP or calcium, but here the white cell count is normal and the platelets are high.
C: An eGFR of 68 is too high to cause meaningful erythropoietin deficiency, which usually appears only when eGFR falls below about 30 to 45.
D: Haemolysis would raise the bilirubin (and LDH and reticulocytes), but his bilirubin is normal.
E: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, often with low platelets, but his MCV is normal and his platelets are raised.
why: Wrong: marrow infiltration lowers the counts or gives a leucoerythroblastic picture, often with a raised ALP or calcium, but here the white cell count is normal, the platelets are high and the ALP and calcium are normal.
Wrong: an eGFR of 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2 is too high to cause erythropoietin deficiency, which usually appears only when eGFR falls below about 30 to 45.
Wrong: haemolysis would raise the bilirubin (and LDH and reticulocytes), but his bilirubin is normal.
Wrong: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, often with low platelets, but his MCV is 87 fL and his platelets are raised.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain that began while she was watching television. Over the past fortnight her known angina has come on with less exertion, and she now needs glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) most days. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin. In the ED she has received aspirin 300 mg, three sublingual GTN doses and intravenous morphine, and an intravenous GTN infusion has been titrated for the past 20 minutes. She still rates the pain 7/10 and is diaphoretic. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg in both arms, respirations 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. Two 12-lead ECGs taken 15 minutes apart show sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. High-sensitivity troponin I, taken 40 minutes after onset, is 9 ng/L (99th percentile for women 16 ng/L). Chest X-ray is normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This woman has a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. She has crescendo angina and prolonged rest pain. Her pain is still going after aspirin, repeated sublingual GTN, opioid and a titrated IV GTN infusion. The 2016 National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guideline, which eTG follows, classes ongoing or recurrent ischaemic pain that does not respond to medical treatment as very high risk. This applies whatever the ECG or troponin shows. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography, with revascularisation if indicated, within 2 hours. Arrange this urgently with cardiology, including the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant. A normal ECG and a normal troponin taken 40 minutes after onset do not lower her risk, because both can be normal early in a myocardial infarction. Repeat troponin, CT coronary angiography and stress testing are for patients whose pain has settled and who are at low or intermediate risk. Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI.
why: Serial troponin helps decide between unstable angina and NSTEMI, but the result would not change her management, because refractory pain already makes her very high risk.
Fibrinolysis gives no benefit and may cause harm in non-ST-elevation ACS, and her ECGs show no ST elevation.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, pain-free patients at low or intermediate risk, not for ongoing ischaemia that needs treatment in the catheter laboratory.
Stress testing is contraindicated while rest pain continues, and putting off assessment until tomorrow is unsafe in very high-risk ACS.

items.stem: A 6-week-old boy has 4 days of projectile non-bilious vomiting. Ultrasound shows pyloric wall thickness 4.5 mm. Venous bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, chloride 90 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis, and he has the typical hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, which makes this a medical emergency but not a surgical one. Following RCH guidance, keep him nil by mouth and give IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose, adding potassium once he passes urine. Pyloromyotomy waits until bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal.
why: Wrong: thickened feeds and GP review suit reflux, but this is confirmed pyloric stenosis with dehydration and alkalosis, so he needs admission and surgery.
Wrong: operating before the alkalosis is corrected risks post-anaesthetic apnoea, because the breathing has slowed to compensate for the alkalosis.
Wrong: a wall thickness of 4.5 mm on ultrasound already confirms the diagnosis, so a contrast study only adds delay and radiation.
Wrong: atropine is a rarely used medical option that works less reliably and is not standard Australian care; pyloromyotomy is the definitive treatment.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm painless nodule in the right thyroid lobe, with palpitations and weight loss. TSH is 0.02 mIU/L (normal 0.4 to 4.0).
items.explanation: If a thyroid nodule comes with a suppressed TSH, the next step is a radionuclide scan (technetium or iodine-123) to find out whether the nodule is hyperfunctioning ("hot"). Hot nodules are very rarely cancerous and usually don't need FNA. Only cold nodules, or nodules with a normal or high TSH, go on to ultrasound-guided FNA based on ultrasound risk features.
why: FNA comes after scintigraphy when TSH is suppressed, because cytology of a hot nodule can look suspicious and lead to needless surgery.
Calcitonin screens for medullary carcinoma and is not a routine first test, especially when the clinical picture is thyrotoxicosis.
CT is used to stage retrosternal extension or airway compression and does not show nodule function or risk of cancer.
Thyroglobulin is used to monitor for recurrence after thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer and cannot tell benign nodules from malignant ones.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with Alzheimer dementia declines surgery for a hip fracture. He accurately explains the risks of refusing and gives consistent reasons. His MMSE is 19/30.
items.explanation: A cognitive screening score does not decide capacity. In Australian law, capacity is specific to each decision and is presumed. He shows that he understands, retains and weighs the information and can communicate a choice, so he may have capacity to refuse despite an MMSE of 19/30.
why: Wrong because the MMSE measures overall cognition, not his ability to make this particular decision, so a low score cannot show incapacity by itself.
Wrong because a guardian or substitute decision-maker is only needed once he has been found to lack capacity for this decision, and that has not happened.
Wrong because a competent adult's informed refusal is legally valid, even if clinicians think the choice is unwise.
Wrong because operating on a patient who may have capacity and has refused would be assault, and the score gives no legal grounds to override him.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin needs two simple dental extractions tomorrow. His INR measured today is 2.6.
items.explanation: An INR of 2.6 is in the therapeutic range and below the usual cut-off of about 3 for simple dental extractions. The extractions can go ahead without stopping warfarin, using local haemostatic measures such as packing, sutures and tranexamic acid mouthwash. Stopping warfarin raises the risk of stroke and gives little benefit, because bleeding after an extraction can be controlled locally.
why: Stopping warfarin for 5 days leaves the patient without anticoagulation and at risk of stroke, and it is not needed when the INR is therapeutic for a minor oral procedure.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin and is kept for very high INRs or active bleeding, not for a planned extraction with a therapeutic INR.
Bridging is only needed when warfarin has to be stopped, and here it does not have to be.
Waiting for a normal INR means stopping anticoagulation, which puts the patient at risk of stroke for no benefit because the current INR is already safe for extraction.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer presents with confusion and polyuria. His corrected calcium is 3.6 mmol/L and he is clinically dehydrated.
items.explanation: Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia of malignancy causes volume depletion. Per eTG, the first step is IV rehydration with sodium chloride 0.9%, which restores kidney perfusion and calcium excretion. An IV bisphosphonate is given once the patient is rehydrated.
why: Zoledronic acid is needed but takes 2 to 4 days to work, and it is nephrotoxic if given before the patient is rehydrated.
Denosumab is kept for hypercalcaemia that does not respond to bisphosphonates or for severe kidney impairment, not for first-line acute treatment.
Furosemide worsens dehydration and is only used for fluid overload after rehydration, not as a routine calcium-lowering drug.
Corticosteroids help mainly in calcitriol-driven hypercalcaemia, such as lymphoma or granulomatous disease, not PTHrP-mediated squamous cancer.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Over this time he has lost 20 kg, has coughed up blood-tinged sputum and his voice has become hoarse. He has COPD, and his triple-therapy inhaler has not helped. He has smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 50 years and worked for decades as a mechanic. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 29/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg and SpO2 is 92% on room air. He has finger clubbing and a hard right supraclavicular lymph node. On the right side of the chest, expansion is reduced, percussion is stony dull and breath sounds are absent. The trachea is deviated to the left. An erect PA chest X-ray, not rotated, shows a large right effusion with a meniscus reaching the 2nd anterior rib, which obscures the right heart border and hilum. The trachea and mediastinum are displaced to the left. The left lung is clear.
items.ask: Which of the following best explains the position of the trachea and mediastinum on this film?
options: Paratracheal nodal mass displacing the airway
items.explanation: The film shows a large right effusion with the trachea and mediastinum pushed to the left, away from the fluid. Being pushed away from the fluid means the effusion has a mass effect: the fluid takes up enough space in the right hemithorax to move the mediastinum across. For this patient, it means the shift is not explained by a major right-sided collapse, so a central obstructing tumour has not pulled the mediastinum back towards the right. It also means the mediastinum is not held in place by pleural tumour. So ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (no more than about 1.5 L at a time) is likely to ease his breathlessness, and it also gives fluid for diagnosis. A contrast CT chest should ideally be done before the effusion is fully drained. If a very large effusion had no shift, or the mediastinum had moved towards the effusion, that would suggest lobar or lung collapse from an endobronchial tumour, or a mediastinum fixed by mesothelioma or malignant nodes. In that case drainage would help less and could cause problems, and bronchoscopy should be considered. Tension pneumothorax is ruled out because the film shows a meniscus, not air.
why: Collapse causes volume loss, which pulls the trachea and mediastinum towards the affected (right) side, not away from it.
A mediastinum encased by pleural tumour, as in mesothelioma, cannot move, so a large effusion would cause little or no shift.
Hyperinflation in COPD affects both lungs and does not push the mediastinum sideways, and the left lung is described as clear.
A paratracheal nodal mass widens the mediastinum and may narrow the trachea, but it would not shift the whole mediastinum away from a large right effusion.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with CT-confirmed subarachnoid haemorrhage deteriorates in the ED. GCS falls from 14 to 10 and pulse to 46/min; BP rises to 210/110 mmHg, with irregular breathing.
items.ask: What do these findings most likely indicate?
items.explanation: Rising BP, a falling heart rate and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad), together with a falling GCS, mean raised intracranial pressure and impending coning. After SAH this is often caused by acute hydrocephalus. Call a rapid response, protect the airway, get an urgent neurosurgeon for an external ventricular drain, and do not chase the BP down.
why: The BP rise is a Cushing reflex that keeps the brain perfused against high intracranial pressure; it is not the main problem, and lowering it hard would worsen ischaemia.
Delayed cerebral ischaemia typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not within hours of it.
Non-convulsive seizures can lower consciousness, but they do not cause hypertension with bradycardia and irregular breathing.
Neurogenic stunned myocardium causes ECG changes, arrhythmias, hypotension or pulmonary oedema, not hypertension with bradycardia and a falling GCS.

items.stem:
A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner to discuss blood test results. She has had four months of tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain of 5 kg. Wrong: hydrogel moistens the wound, which suits sloughy wounds with good blood supply, but it softens dry gangrene and can turn it into wet, infected gangrene.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl is being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis. Five hours into the insulin infusion she develops headache and irritability. Her heart rate falls from 130 to 60/min. BGL 13 mmol/L.

items.stem:
A 61-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky central abdominal pain and repeated bilious vomiting. She has not passed stool or flatus for 30 hours. She had an open hysterectomy 12 years ago. She takes amlodipine for hypertension. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry. The abdomen is distended, with tinkling bowel sounds and mild generalised tenderness but no guarding. The hernial orifices are normal. She has not passed urine in 3 hours. Results are:
Na+ 132 mmol/L (135–145)
K+ 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
Cl− 89 mmol/L (95–110)
Urea 13.6 mmol/L (2.5–7.5)
Creatinine 118 µmol/L (45–90)
Venous gas: pH 7.48, pCO2 47 mm Hg, HCO3− 33 mmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L
CT shows dilated small bowel with a transition point under the scar and no features of ischaemia. A nasogastric tube is placed.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous fluid to start?
items.explanation: This woman has adhesive small bowel obstruction. Her blood results show a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis: pH 7.48, HCO3− 33 mmol/L, Cl− 89 mmol/L and K+ 3.1 mmol/L. The anion gap is normal (132 − [89 + 33] = 10), and the pCO2 of 47 mm Hg is the expected respiratory compensation (about 0.7 × 9 ≈ 6 mm Hg above 40). She also has a prerenal acute kidney injury, with urea raised out of proportion to creatinine, a tachycardia and no urine output. This pattern comes from vomiting and nasogastric loss of gastric acid (HCl) together with fluid loss. The kidney then holds on to sodium and bicarbonate and loses potassium (contraction alkalosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism). The alkalosis is chloride-responsive: it corrects only when chloride and volume are replaced. So the right fluid is 0.9% saline (154 mmol/L chloride) with potassium chloride added, usually 20 to 40 mmol/L, for both resuscitation and replacement, with fluid balance and electrolytes monitored. Hartmann's and Plasma-Lyte contain less chloride and carry anions that the body turns into bicarbonate (lactate, acetate, gluconate), and 5% glucose and albumin do not replace what she has lost.
why: Hartmann's has less chloride (111 mmol/L) and only 5 mmol/L potassium, and its lactate is turned into bicarbonate, which makes the alkalosis worse.
Plasma-Lyte 148 has even less chloride (98 mmol/L), and its acetate and gluconate are turned into bicarbonate, so it does not correct a hypochloraemic alkalosis.
Albumin replaces neither chloride nor potassium, has no proven benefit over crystalloid for this kind of volume loss, and costs more.
5% glucose is mostly free water that does not stay in the circulation, so it will not correct her volume loss, and it will make her hyponatraemia worse.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has been ventilated in ICU for 30 hours after a severe traumatic brain injury. He has no brainstem reflexes and no spontaneous breathing. Core temperature is 33.8°C.
items.explanation: Under the ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation, core temperature must be above 35°C before brain death can be determined, because hypothermia itself depresses brainstem function. He must be rewarmed, and the clinical tests done only once all preconditions are met.

Perfusion imaging is used when the clinical exam cannot be done or trusted for lasting reasons, not for hypothermia that can be corrected.
A reversible cause is present, so the coma cannot be called irreversible at this point.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 days of lower abdominal colic, gross tympanic distension and no flatus since yesterday. He vomited once today. Rectum is empty.
items.ask: Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Early obstipation, marked distension and late vomiting point to large bowel obstruction. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the key investigation. It confirms the obstruction and shows its level and cause (cancer, diverticular stricture or volvulus), and it picks up complications such as caecal dilatation, ischaemia or perforation.

Colonoscopy is not used to diagnose acute obstruction because insufflating an obstructed, distended colon risks perforation.
Ultrasound is limited by gas in a distended bowel and cannot reliably show the level or cause of a colonic obstruction.
A water-soluble contrast enema can show the site of blockage but has mostly been replaced by CT, which also assesses the rest of the abdomen and complications.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who etches glass has severe throbbing pain in two fingertips after hydrofluoric acid leaked into his glove. Skin is only mildly red and has been irrigated with water.
items.explanation: Hydrofluoric acid soaks deep into tissue, and its fluoride ions bind calcium. This causes pain far worse than the skin looks, plus deep tissue death. After water irrigation, apply 2.5% calcium gluconate gel and massage it in repeatedly until the pain goes; if pain persists, give calcium by local injection or by intra-arterial infusion.

Putting a base on the skin to neutralise an acid is not recommended, because the reaction gives off heat and does not bind fluoride.
Opioids only mask pain, so you lose the main sign that guides calcium treatment, and the fluoride damage keeps going.
Debridement is reserved for clearly dead tissue after calcium treatment has been given, not as first-line care.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man is ready for discharge after IV diuresis for decompensated heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy, LVEF 30%. He asks how to detect fluid reaccumulation early at home.
items.explanation: Recurrent congestion is the main early risk after a heart failure admission, and fluid builds up in the body before symptoms appear. The Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidelines advise weighing every morning after voiding, on the same scales, and seeing the GP promptly if weight rises by more than 2 kg over 2 days or swelling or breathlessness gets worse. Chest pain or severe breathlessness means calling 000.

Oxygen saturation usually falls only once pulmonary oedema is established, so it does not give early warning.
NT-proBNP guides diagnosis and specialist review; a monthly test is too infrequent for home monitoring and not practical.
Blood pressure checks help with titrating drugs, but blood pressure does not track fluid build-up reliably.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to his general practitioner to review his test results. For 18 months he has had worsening breathlessness on exertion and now has to stop after about 200 m on flat ground. He also has a daily cough with clear sputum. Last winter he had one flare-up, treated in the community with oral prednisolone, and he has never been admitted to hospital. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history. He started varenicline 2 weeks ago and has set a quit date. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He uses salbutamol 200 micrograms via a spacer as needed, now on most days, and his technique is good. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 94% on room air. Air entry is reduced and there is scattered expiratory wheeze. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.56 and FEV1 is 55% of predicted, with no significant bronchodilator response. Blood eosinophils are 0.15 x10^9/L (reference 0.0 to 0.5). He has been referred to pulmonary rehabilitation.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his medicines?
items.explanation: This man has spirometry-confirmed COPD: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is below 0.7. His FEV1 of 55% predicted puts him in the moderate range in COPD-X (40 to 59%). His breathlessness persists despite a short-acting reliever, and he already has the non-drug measures under way: varenicline with a quit date, and a referral to pulmonary rehabilitation. COPD-X and eTG recommend adding a long-acting bronchodilator for persistent symptoms. A long-acting muscarinic antagonist such as tiotropium, taken once daily and kept alongside the as-needed reliever, is a standard first choice. It improves breathlessness, exercise tolerance and quality of life, and it reduces flare-ups. Inhaled corticosteroids are added only for repeated flare-ups despite long-acting bronchodilators, especially when eosinophils are raised. He has had one community-treated flare-up and his eosinophils are 0.15 x10^9/L, so a steroid is not indicated. Triple therapy, theophylline and long-term macrolides belong to later steps, if at all. Recheck his inhaler technique and review his symptoms after starting the new inhaler.
why: Wrong: guidelines do not recommend an inhaled corticosteroid alone in COPD, because it does not help breathlessness and raises the risk of pneumonia.
Wrong: triple therapy is for people who keep having flare-ups despite dual long-acting bronchodilators, and he has had one mild flare-up and his eosinophils are low.
Wrong: theophylline is a late add-on with a narrow therapeutic range, many drug interactions and less benefit than inhaled long-acting bronchodilators.
Wrong: long-term macrolide treatment is a specialist option for frequent flare-ups despite optimal inhaled therapy, and it carries risks of resistance, hearing loss and QT prolongation.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man, a retired plumber with asbestos exposure, has right shoulder pain and weight loss. CT shows a 5 cm peripheral right apical mass without mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
items.ask: Best test to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: A peripheral apical (superior sulcus) mass suspicious for lung cancer needs tissue for diagnosis. With no enlarged nodes, a percutaneous CT-guided core biopsy gives the highest yield and enough tissue for histology and molecular testing. This follows the Australian optimal care pathway for lung cancer.
why: Bronchoscopic biopsy has a low yield for peripheral apical lesions, which lie beyond the reach of the bronchoscope.
Sputum cytology is insensitive for peripheral tumours, and a negative result would not exclude cancer.
EBUS sampling is used for enlarged mediastinal or hilar nodes, and none are present here.
PET-CT is used for staging and cannot give a tissue diagnosis.
