items.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to a general practice because his eyes have been yellow for 3 days. Ten days ago he developed fevers, anorexia, nausea and malaise, followed by dark urine and pale stools. Five weeks ago he returned from a 3-week backpacking trip through Vietnam, where he ate street food and had ice in his drinks. He did not have a pre-travel consultation or any travel vaccines. His travel companion became jaundiced last week. He takes no medicines or supplements and rarely drinks alcohol. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse 88/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. He has scleral icterus and a tender, smooth liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin. He is alert, with no asterixis. Results: bilirubin 102 µmol/L (<20), ALT 1240 U/L (<40), AST 610 U/L (<40), ALP 190 U/L (30–110), GGT 85 U/L (<50), INR 1.0 (0.9–1.2), haemoglobin 141 g/L, white cell count 4.8 x10^9/L and platelets 236 x10^9/L. Abdominal ultrasound shows a mildly enlarged liver, no gallstones and a normal-calibre common bile duct.
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This unvaccinated traveller has a clear enteric exposure in South-East Asia. He became unwell about 4 weeks after the exposure, which fits the incubation period of hepatitis A (about 2 to 7 weeks). He had a febrile prodrome followed by jaundice, and his travel companion is also jaundiced, which suggests a shared source. His liver tests show a hepatocellular pattern: ALT about 30 times the upper limit, far more raised than ALP and GGT, with ALT above AST. His INR is normal and he is alert, so there is no sign of acute liver failure. The ultrasound excludes biliary obstruction. The most likely diagnosis is acute hepatitis A. The test that confirms it is hepatitis A IgM antibody. IgM is present when symptoms start and stays positive for about 3 to 6 months, so a positive result means recent infection. This is the first-line test for acute hepatitis in Australian guidance (eTG, CDNA SoNG). Confirmed hepatitis A must be notified to the public health unit. Close contacts who are not immune should get post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks of their last exposure.
why: Thick and thin films are needed for fever in a traveller back from a malaria area, but malaria does not cause conjugated jaundice with ALT over 1000 when the haemoglobin and platelets are normal, so films will not confirm this diagnosis.

Hepatitis E is also spread enterically in Asia, but hepatitis A is more common in unvaccinated travellers and rarely spreads between people; guidelines test for hepatitis A IgM first and hepatitis E only if that is negative.
Total hepatitis A antibody is positive after past infection or vaccination as well as current infection, so on its own it cannot show that this illness is acute hepatitis A.
MRCP looks for stones or strictures in the bile ducts, and it is not indicated here because the ultrasound shows a normal-calibre duct and the liver tests point to hepatitis rather than obstruction.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and 1 day of vomiting. He has no past medical history. He weighs 36 kg. His first venous blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34.0 mmol/L and sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L and urea is 13.2 mmol/L. Fluid replacement is started, and 1 hour later an insulin infusion is started at 0.1 units/kg/h. Five hours after arrival he says he has a severe headache, vomits, and becomes irritable and confused. His pulse is 58/min (130/min on arrival), blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min, SpO2 is 98% on room air and temperature is 36.9 °C. GCS is 11 (E3 V3 M5). His pupils are equal and reactive. Repeat glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and sodium is 129 mmol/L. The head of the bed is raised and the fluid rate is reduced.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain now
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV over 1 hour
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Cease the insulin infusion until review
items.explanation: This boy has severe DKA as his first presentation of type 1 diabetes. He has the main risk factors for cerebral oedema: young age, new diagnosis, pH below 7.1, a high urea, and a sodium that is falling instead of rising as the glucose comes down. Several hours into treatment he has a headache, vomiting, a falling GCS and a new low heart rate with high blood pressure (Cushing response). This is a clinical diagnosis of cerebral oedema. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat it straight away, without waiting for imaging. Raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 20%) IV over 20 minutes. Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is an alternative. Call ICU early for airway support, and do a CT only after he is stable, to look for other causes such as a clot or bleed. CT now is wrong because imaging delays treatment that can save his life, and cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically. Sodium bicarbonate is wrong because it does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema. Dexamethasone is wrong because steroids do not help this kind of brain swelling and they make hyperglycaemia worse. Stopping the insulin is wrong because the ketosis needs ongoing insulin to clear; the rate may be lowered, but the infusion should not be stopped to treat cerebral oedema.
why: Wrong: CT delays urgent treatment for a diagnosis made clinically; image only once he is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
Wrong: corticosteroids have no role in cerebral oedema from DKA and would worsen his hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: insulin is still needed to clear the ketosis, and stopping it does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with adhesive small bowel obstruction is managed with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids. Overnight her colicky pain becomes constant, with localised tenderness, heart rate 124/min and temperature 38.1°C.
items.explanation: In adhesive small bowel obstruction, colicky pain that becomes constant, together with localised tenderness, tachycardia and fever, points to strangulation with ischaemia. A normal lactate does not rule it out. She needs urgent CT with IV contrast and an early surgical review for laparotomy, because conservative management has failed.

Perforation usually comes after ischaemia and causes generalised peritonitis with free gas, not localised tenderness alone.
Paralytic ileus gives painless or mildly uncomfortable distension with absent bowel sounds, not fever and constant localised pain.
Mesenteric venous thrombosis is a separate cause of ischaemia in prothrombotic patients, not the usual complication of a mechanical adhesive obstruction.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a sudden, severe occipital headache that began while he was jogging. Two weeks ago he had a severe headache that settled within 30 minutes. He has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, treated with perindopril. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 82/min, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 (E3 V4 M6). He has neck stiffness and bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages on fundoscopy, and no focal deficit. INR is 1.0 and platelets are 245 x10^9/L. Non-contrast CT shows diffuse blood in the basal cisterns, spreading into the ventricles, with dilated temporal horns. CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Forty-five minutes later he vomits. His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 48/min, blood pressure 204/96 mm Hg and respirations 12/min and irregular. His pupils are still equal and reactive.
items.ask: Which of the following best explains the change in his vital signs?
items.explanation: This man has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood has spread into his ventricles, and the dilated temporal horns show early hydrocephalus. Since arrival his GCS has fallen. He now has a rising systolic pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing. This is Cushing's triad, a late sign that intracranial pressure is raised and the brainstem is being compressed, which means coning is imminent. Equal pupils do not rule this out, because pupil changes can come late. Do not read the rising blood pressure as something to treat on its own. It is the brain's attempt to keep up cerebral perfusion pressure, and lowering it hard could make ischaemia worse. Under eTG guidance and the Between the Flags criteria, this needs an immediate rapid response call, airway assessment, the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees, and an urgent neurosurgical review for an external ventricular drain. Delayed cerebral ischaemia usually happens on days 3 to 14, not within hours of the bleed. A hypertensive emergency does not explain the slow heart rate or the fall in GCS, and on arrival his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg. A vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure. Neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge typically causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and heart failure.
why: Wrong: delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not 3 hours after the headache began.
Wrong: a hypertensive emergency would not cause a falling heart rate or irregular breathing, and his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg before his GCS fell.
Wrong: a vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure, and it would not cause a lasting fall in GCS or irregular breathing.
Wrong: neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge usually causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema, not a slow heart rate with severe hypertension.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD and 50 pack-years presents with a large right pleural effusion. SpO2 is 89% on room air. A non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min is applied.
items.explanation: In COPD, high-concentration oxygen can cause hypercapnic respiratory failure and acidosis. This happens because of worsening V/Q mismatch, the Haldane effect and reduced respiratory drive. TSANZ guidelines advise titrating oxygen with nasal prongs or a Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92%.

Absorption atelectasis from a high FiO2 does occur, but it matters much less clinically than CO2 retention in COPD.
Pulmonary oxygen toxicity needs prolonged exposure to a very high FiO2, usually over 24 to 48 hours, so it is not the immediate risk.
Supplemental oxygen does not cause pneumothorax; pleural aspiration is the procedure that carries that risk.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man is on the cardiology ward of a regional hospital, waiting for transfer for coronary angiography. He was admitted 18 hours ago with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and has no pain now. Overnight telemetry has shown frequent multifocal ventricular ectopic beats and two runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, each 5 to 7 beats long. He has hypertension treated with indapamide. Since admission he has been given aspirin, ticagrelor, therapeutic enoxaparin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. His blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 and a QTc of 470 ms. Results: hs-troponin I 1960 ng/L (less than 26), K+ 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), Mg2+ 0.58 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), creatinine 90 µmol/L (60 to 110).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce his risk of ventricular fibrillation before angiography?
options: Intravenous amiodarone loading dose, then maintenance infusion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate, then potassium chloride infusion
Intravenous lidocaine bolus, then prophylactic infusion
Oral slow-release potassium chloride tablets alone
Oral flecainide twice daily until angiography
items.explanation: This man has an evolving NSTEMI and is waiting for angiography. Ventricular ectopy and non-sustained VT on telemetry, a borderline long QTc, and low potassium and magnesium from his thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) put him at high risk of ventricular fibrillation. In acute coronary syndrome, Australian ACS guidance and ANZCOR advise correcting electrolytes promptly, aiming for potassium of at least 4.0 mmol/L (4.0 to 5.0) and magnesium of at least 1.0 mmol/L. Give magnesium first, for example magnesium sulfate 10 to 20 mmol IV over about an hour. Low magnesium makes low potassium hard to correct, because the kidneys keep losing potassium, and magnesium also stabilises the myocardium when the QT is long. Then give IV potassium chloride at a safe ward rate (for example 10 mmol/h through a peripheral line) with ECG monitoring, recheck the levels, and stop the indapamide. Keep him on continuous monitoring, continue the beta-blocker, and arrange early angiography to treat the ischaemic cause. Prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs are not recommended in ACS.
why: Prophylactic amiodarone for asymptomatic non-sustained VT after myocardial infarction does not lower mortality and is not recommended; amiodarone is kept for sustained or recurrent haemodynamically important VT, or for refractory VF during cardiac arrest.
Prophylactic lidocaine in acute myocardial infarction reduces VF but increases mortality, mainly from asystole, so it is no longer used.
Oral potassium alone works too slowly in a patient at high arrhythmic risk, and it does not correct the low magnesium that will keep the potassium from rising.
Flecainide, a class Ic drug, is contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease because it increased arrhythmic death after myocardial infarction in the CAST trial.

items.stem: A 10-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote Kimberley community has acute rheumatic fever with migratory polyarthritis and an ASO titre of 800 IU/mL. Echocardiography shows no carditis.
items.ask: Secondary prophylaxis mainly prevents which complication?
items.explanation: Each new group A streptococcal infection can trigger acute rheumatic fever again, and each episode adds valve damage. Under the Australian ARF/RHD guideline, monthly IM benzathine benzylpenicillin for at least 10 years is given to prevent recurrences and the chronic rheumatic heart disease they cause. This matters even when there is no carditis at first presentation.

Glomerulonephritis is a separate post-streptococcal illness (often after skin infection) that is not prevented by ARF secondary prophylaxis.
Arthritis in acute rheumatic fever goes away without lasting joint damage, and Jaccoud arthropathy is rare, so it is not what prophylaxis targets.
Rheumatic carditis mainly damages the valves rather than causing dilated cardiomyopathy, so this is not the main outcome prevented.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man sees his general practitioner to review results. For 6 months he has had increasing breathlessness on exertion and central chest tightness when climbing stairs, which settles with rest. Last week he nearly fainted while walking uphill. He has hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia and takes irbesartan 150 mg daily. His blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. The carotid pulse is slow rising. There is a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space that radiates to both carotids, with a soft second heart sound. Fine crackles are heard at both lung bases, and there is no peripheral oedema. A transthoracic echocardiogram shows a heavily calcified trileaflet aortic valve, peak velocity 4.5 m/s, mean gradient 50 mm Hg, valve area 0.7 cm², concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and an ejection fraction of 62%. He has been referred urgently to cardiology for heart team assessment. He asks for something to relieve his chest tightness while he waits.
items.ask: Which of the following medicines is most likely to cause a serious adverse event in this patient before his valve is replaced?
items.explanation: This man has symptomatic severe calcific aortic stenosis, with breathlessness, angina and presyncope on exertion, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. With a fixed outflow obstruction and a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle, cardiac output cannot rise to make up for a fall in preload or afterload. Nitrates such as sublingual glyceryl trinitrate cause venous and arterial dilatation. That lowers preload, so the stiff ventricle underfills, and the patient can develop profound hypotension, syncope, worsening myocardial ischaemia and even cardiac arrest. eTG and the 2025 ESC/EACTS valvular guidelines advise avoiding nitrates and other potent vasodilators in severe aortic stenosis. They also advise cautious diuresis for congestion while the patient waits for TAVI or SAVR. The definitive treatment for his angina is valve replacement, not antianginal drugs. Low-dose furosemide, used carefully, is appropriate for congestion. Atorvastatin is safe and treats his hypercholesterolaemia. Paracetamol is a safe analgesic with no haemodynamic effect. Tiotropium has no meaningful effect on preload or afterload.
why: Low-dose loop diuretic, used cautiously with monitoring, is the recommended way to relieve pulmonary congestion while he waits for valve replacement.
A statin is safe in aortic stenosis and treats his hypercholesterolaemia, although it does not slow the valve disease.
Paracetamol has no vasodilator or negative inotropic effect, so it is safe in severe aortic stenosis.
A long-acting antimuscarinic inhaler does not change preload or afterload, so it carries no particular haemodynamic risk here, even if it is not indicated.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with hypertension has sudden, severe, tearing pain between her shoulder blades that was worst at onset. Left arm BP is 164/90 mmHg and right arm BP is 132/80 mmHg.
items.ask: Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Sudden tearing interscapular pain with a difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms gives a high aortic dissection detection risk score (ADD-RS). A D-dimer result should not be used to rule out dissection at this level of risk.

A CT pulmonary angiogram is timed for the pulmonary arteries, so it may not opacify the aorta well enough to assess it, and pulmonary embolism does not cause a difference in blood pressure between the arms.

items.stem: A 4-week-old breastfed girl has had jaundice since day 3. She is feeding and gaining weight well. Her stools are pale cream and her urine stains the nappy yellow.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man, an electrician, sees his general practitioner because of 5 months of daytime sleepiness. He dozes off while watching television and in the afternoons, and he wakes unrefreshed despite 8 hours in bed. His wife reports loud snoring every night, with pauses in his breathing followed by gasping. He has had no sudden muscle weakness with laughter or anger, and he denies sleepiness while driving. He drinks 3 standard drinks most evenings and does not smoke. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. Blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. BMI is 34 kg/m2, neck circumference is 44 cm and the oropharynx is crowded. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 13 (normal 10 or less), STOP-Bang score 6/8 and OSA50 score 7/10. Full blood count, TSH and electrolytes are normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This man very probably has obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). He snores, his wife has seen him stop breathing, he is sleepy in the daytime, he has obesity with a large neck and a crowded oropharynx, he has hypertension, and he drinks alcohol in the evening. Before treatment starts, the diagnosis has to be confirmed and graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI). His Epworth score is 8 or more and his STOP-Bang (4 or more) and OSA50 (5 or more) scores are high-risk. This meets the MBS item 12250 criteria, so a GP can refer him directly for an unattended Level 2 polysomnography done at home. Australasian Sleep Association and eTG guidance say this test is the right one for a patient with a high pre-test probability and no major other illness. Treatment then depends on the AHI: CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, and everyone gets lifestyle measures (weight loss, less alcohol, side sleeping) and advice on driving. Overnight oximetry alone misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels and cannot measure the AHI, so it is not enough to diagnose OSA. CPAP, a splint or a wake-promoting drug should not be started before the diagnosis and severity are known.
why: Oximetry alone cannot measure the AHI and misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels, so it is not recommended for diagnosing OSA.
CPAP is first line only once a sleep study has confirmed moderate to severe OSA, and it should not be started on screening scores alone.
A mandibular advancement splint is an alternative for confirmed mild to moderate OSA or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, so it is not a first step before diagnosis.
Modafinil is used only for sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of confirmed OSA, and it does nothing for the airway obstruction.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman, 2 hours after hysteroscopy and curettage, has severe lower abdominal pain and guarding. Curettings contained yellow fatty tissue. BP 90/55 mmHg despite 1 L crystalloid.
items.ask: Which investigation will most likely confirm the diagnosis?

items.stem: A 10-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability is brought to his general practitioner by his mother because he has become aggressive at home and at school over the past 4 weeks. He has hit his teacher, slaps his own belly and keeps pulling at the left side of his face. He has stopped eating toast and apples. His bowels open every 4 to 5 days with hard stools and occasional soiling. His risperidone was increased to 0.5 mg twice daily 6 weeks ago. His temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 94/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. He has a firm, mildly tender mass in the left iliac fossa. A lower left first permanent molar has a large carious cavity and is tender to percussion, and the gum next to it is red and swollen with no fluctuance. He has no facial swelling or trismus. He has a fine tremor and mild cogwheel rigidity at both wrists. A urine dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites.
items.ask: In addition to starting treatment for constipation, which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: When a child with intellectual disability suddenly changes his behaviour, look for pain or illness first, because he cannot describe his symptoms. This boy has two painful causes. The first is faecal loading: hard stools every 4 to 5 days, soiling, a firm left iliac fossa mass and slapping his own belly. The RCH guideline says constipation is a clinical diagnosis, so it needs treatment, not imaging. The second is a probable periapical (dental) abscess: he pulls at the left of his face, refuses crunchy food, and has a carious molar that is tender to percussion with red, swollen gum next to it. Imaging confirms this. An orthopantomogram (or a periapical film taken by a dentist) shows the periapical lucency, the depth of the decay and how far infection has spread. It then guides urgent dental treatment, either drainage, pulp treatment or extraction, while he gets weight-based analgesia. Plain abdominal X-ray: the RCH advises against it because constipation is diagnosed clinically and the X-ray does not change management. Urine microscopy and culture: the dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites, and his extra wetting fits a loaded rectum pressing on the bladder. Serum creatine kinase: he is afebrile with normal observations and only mild extrapyramidal signs, so neuroleptic malignant syndrome is unlikely; his risperidone needs a medication review instead. Thyroid function tests: thyroid disease does not explain a tender carious tooth or a faecal mass, and it would not cause a sudden 4-week change with focal pain signs.
why: Constipation is a clinical diagnosis, and the RCH advises against abdominal X-ray because it does not change management.
The dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites, so a UTI is unlikely, and the mild wetting fits rectal loading.
He is afebrile with normal observations and only mild extrapyramidal signs, so neuroleptic malignant syndrome is not suspected and his risperidone needs review instead.
Thyroid disease would not explain the focal dental findings or the faecal mass, so it would not confirm a cause of this sudden change.

items.stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father with 4 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit is milky and has never been green. He feeds eagerly straight after vomiting and has had 2 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. He was born at term and is formula fed. He weighs 4.5 kg, down from 4.9 kg 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 172/min, respirations 38/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is drowsy but rouses to voice. His hands and feet are cool and capillary refill time is 3 seconds. A peripheral cannula is placed. Venous gas: pH 7.53 (7.32 to 7.42), bicarbonate 37 mmol/L (20 to 28), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (under 2.0), Na 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 2.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), Cl 86 mmol/L (95 to 110), glucose 4.3 mmol/L. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 18 mm.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: 0.45% sodium chloride with 2.5% glucose at 18 mL/h intravenously
0.9% sodium chloride 45 mL intravenously over 15 minutes
Potassium chloride 2.25 mmol intravenously over 1 hour

items.explanation: This boy has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The ultrasound shows a muscle wall of 5 mm or more (abnormal is 3 mm or more) and a channel of 18 mm (abnormal is 15 mm or more), and he has the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. He is also in compensated shock: he is tachycardic, drowsy and cool at the hands and feet, with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, while his blood pressure is still normal. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not a surgical emergency. The first step is to treat the shock. Keep him nil by mouth and give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (45 mL for 4.5 kg), then reassess. After that, give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, and add potassium once he is passing urine (RCH Pyloric stenosis, Dehydration and Intravenous fluids guidelines). Surgery waits until the bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal, because operating while he is still alkalotic risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

Wrong: potassium is replaced only after perfusion is restored and he is passing urine, and it does not treat the shock.
Wrong: his low potassium and alkalosis are the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which causes a high potassium and an acidosis, so steroids are not needed.
Wrong: pyloromyotomy should wait until shock and the alkalosis are corrected, because operating sooner risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has two weeks of facial swelling, morning headache worse on bending forward, and dilated veins over his upper chest wall.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman, a school teacher, returns to her general practitioner for review of a duodenal ulcer. Last month she presented with burning epigastric pain that woke her at night. A non-contrast CT brain is normal. A lumbar puncture is done 1 hour after the first antibiotic doses. CSF results:

Opening pressure 28 cmH2O (10 to 20)
Appearance: turbid
White cell count 1200 ×10^6/L (below 5), 85% polymorphs
Red cell count 3 ×10^6/L
Protein 1.6 g/L (0.15 to 0.45)
Glucose 1.5 mmol/L; paired plasma glucose 8.0 mmol/L
Gram stain: no organisms seen
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the Gram stain result?
options: A bacterial cause is excluded, and the antibiotics can be stopped
A viral cause is confirmed, and aciclovir alone should be given
A fungal cause is suggested, and amphotericin should be added
The sample is probably contaminated, and the procedure should be repeated
A bacterial cause remains likely, and the present therapy should continue

That rate drops after antibiotics have been given, as here, and Listeria monocytogenes shows on Gram stain in only about a third of cases. Listeria is a real concern because she has been on corticosteroids for 6 weeks. Under eTG, she should stay on empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria), with dexamethasone, until the culture and bacterial PCR come back. Treatment can then be narrowed or stopped on those results, not on the Gram stain.

Wrong: cryptococcal and other fungal meningitis usually cause a lymphocytic CSF with a slower onset and are diagnosed by cryptococcal antigen or India ink, not by an absent Gram stain result.
Wrong: contamination would add organisms rather than hide them, the very low red cell count rules out a traumatic tap, and repeating the lumbar puncture would add risk without changing management.

Treating the ST depression as an acute coronary syndrome with anticoagulants, antiplatelets or thrombolysis can cause rupture, tamponade or catastrophic bleeding. These drugs must be held until dissection has been excluded.

In a hypertensive patient, an IV beta blocker is the first-line anti-impulse treatment, aiming for a heart rate of about 60 and a systolic BP of 100 to 120 mmHg.
An antiemetic is safe here and helps prevent vomiting, which would otherwise raise blood pressure and the stress on the aortic wall.
Paracetamol is a safe extra pain reliever with no effect on bleeding or blood pressure in a dissection.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman admitted to the ward with HSV-1 encephalitis confirmed on CSF PCR starts IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly. She is drowsy with poor oral intake. Creatinine is 72 µmol/L.
items.ask: Most important adverse effect to monitor?
items.explanation: High-dose IV aciclovir can crystallise in the renal tubules and cause crystal nephropathy and acute kidney injury. The risk is higher in older patients, with dehydration such as her poor oral intake, and with other nephrotoxins. eTG advises keeping her well hydrated, checking creatinine regularly and adjusting the dose to renal function, which also prevents aciclovir neurotoxicity that could be mistaken for worsening encephalitis.

Ototoxicity is a typical adverse effect of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics, not of aciclovir.
Severe hypokalaemia is typical of amphotericin B, not of aciclovir.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with two days of vomiting, a distended abdomen and dry mucosa. Venous gas: pH 7.43, pCO2 46 mmHg, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L.
items.explanation: The answer is metabolic alkalosis. A high bicarbonate with a pH at the top of the range shows a primary metabolic alkalosis, with a small compensatory rise in pCO2. It comes from losing gastric acid and chloride in the vomit, made worse by volume depletion and hypokalaemia, and it is treated with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and potassium.
why: The pCO2 of 46 mmHg is the expected respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis, and the pH is not acidaemic.
A respiratory alkalosis would need a low pCO2, but here it is raised.
Lactic acidosis would lower the bicarbonate, but here it is raised.
A hyperchloraemic acidosis would lower the bicarbonate and typically follows diarrhoea or large saline loads, not vomiting.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents after her partner manually strangled her last night until she briefly lost consciousness. She has neck bruising and facial petechiae; neurological examination is normal.
items.ask: Which delayed complication is most important to exclude?

Laryngeal fracture shows up straight away with hoarseness, stridor or crepitus, not as a silent delayed problem.
Vocal cord palsy would cause hoarseness and is not the dangerous or delayed threat to her life.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation had NIPT showing a high chance of trisomy 16. Amniocentesis shows a normal fetal karyotype, and her ultrasound shows normal fetal anatomy.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had 18 hours of vomiting and watery, non-bloody diarrhoea after minding her unwell grandson. She takes perindopril and metformin. HR 118/min, BP 98/60 mmHg; her abdomen is soft.

items.stem:
A 66-year-old man sees his general practitioner about 4 months of looser, more frequent stools, now three times daily. On several occasions there has been dark red blood mixed through the stool. He reports tiredness but no weight loss or abdominal pain. He had rubber band ligation of internal haemorrhoids 5 years ago. A National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit arrived last week, and he asks whether he should complete it; his kit 2 years ago was negative. He takes no regular medicines, including no aspirin or anti-inflammatory drugs. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination is normal. Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy show small, non-bleeding internal haemorrhoids and no mass. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130–180)
MCV 74 fL (80–100)
Ferritin 6 µg/L (30–500)
TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA negative
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Complete the immunochemical faecal occult blood test kit
Oral iron and a repeat blood count in 8 weeks
Repeat rubber band ligation of the internal haemorrhoids
CT colonography as the first investigation
items.explanation: This man has a new, ongoing change in bowel habit at 66, blood mixed through the stool, and iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 104 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L). He takes no NSAIDs and has no other obvious source of blood loss. Colorectal cancer must be assumed until it is excluded. The Cancer Council Australia optimal care pathway says a symptomatic patient should be referred for urgent diagnostic colonoscopy. GESA guidance on iron deficiency says a man or a postmenopausal woman with iron deficiency anaemia needs both colonoscopy and gastroscopy (bidirectional endoscopy), because there can be a lesion in both the upper and lower gut. A negative coeliac test does not remove the need for gastroscopy. Small haemorrhoids that are not bleeding do not explain the change in habit or the anaemia, and a normal rectal examination does not exclude a lesion higher in the colon. An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. A negative result would falsely reassure him, and the negative kit 2 years ago tells us nothing about his current symptoms.
why: An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; he has red-flag symptoms and anaemia, so he needs a diagnostic test, and a negative result would falsely reassure him.
Giving iron alone without finding the source would delay the diagnosis of a likely gastrointestinal cancer, and a rise in haemoglobin would hide the problem.
Small haemorrhoids that are not bleeding do not explain blood mixed through the stool, the change in habit or the iron deficiency, so treating them misses the likely cause.
CT colonography is a second-line option when colonoscopy cannot be done; it cannot take a biopsy or examine the upper gut, which this patient's iron deficiency anaemia requires.

items.stem: A 31-year-old surgical registrar arrives for an overnight shift smelling of alcohol, slurring his words and unsteady on his feet. You are the intern rostered with him.

Quietly covering for him hides the impairment, leaves you without senior support, and fails your duty to report.
Security is not the right first contact for a colleague who is impaired but not violent; the clinical chain of command is.

items.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote community has facial swelling and cola-coloured urine three weeks after infected scabies. BP 130/85 mmHg. Urinalysis shows red cell casts; serum C3 is low.
items.explanation: Red cell casts show a nephritic picture. With a low C3 two to four weeks after a streptococcal skin infection, this points to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is common in remote Aboriginal communities where scabies and impetigo are endemic. Confirm with ASOT and anti-DNase B, recheck C3 at 6 to 8 weeks to make sure it has returned to normal, and notify public health so household contacts can be screened and given treatment or prophylaxis.

Minimal change disease causes nephrotic-range proteinuria without red cell casts, and the complement level is normal.
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome follows a diarrhoeal illness and shows haemolytic anaemia and low platelets; it does not cause a low C3 with casts after a skin infection.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis also lowers C3, but the C3 stays low beyond 8 weeks; a typical post-infective onset makes it far less likely.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 70 minutes after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. She was last seen well at 08:10. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension, treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily and perindopril. Her last apixaban dose was at 07:30 today. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 92/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168/94 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has non-fluent aphasia, a right facial droop and right arm power of 1/5 (NIHSS 15). Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L (150-400), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2) and APTT 30 seconds (25-38). Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a left M1 occlusion, and CT perfusion shows a 10 mL core within a 90 mL perfusion deficit. An apixaban-specific anti-Xa level is pending.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This woman has an acute left middle cerebral artery stroke from a proximal (M1) large vessel occlusion. She is within 6 hours of last known well, has a disabling deficit (NIHSS 15), and has a small core with a large salvageable penumbra. The Stroke Foundation Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines recommend endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion in this setting, whether or not the patient can have thrombolysis. Anticoagulation does not rule it out. She took apixaban about 2 hours ago, well within 48 hours, so IV thrombolysis is contraindicated unless a drug-specific anti-Xa level shows no meaningful anticoagulant effect. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically relevant apixaban effect. Do not wait for the pending level before the clot retrieval pathway is started, because every minute of delay costs brain tissue. Other care in the meantime: keep her nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and do not lower blood pressure routinely. The value of 168/94 mm Hg is already below the 185/110 threshold used for reperfusion therapy.
why: Wrong: she took apixaban within 48 hours, and a normal INR and APTT do not exclude a significant apixaban effect, so thrombolysis carries an unacceptable risk of haemorrhage until a drug-specific level shows no effect.
Wrong: idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran and has no effect on apixaban, a factor Xa inhibitor.
Wrong: guidelines do not support reversing a DOAC with prothrombin complex concentrate so that thrombolysis can be given, as this adds thrombotic risk and delay without proven benefit.
Wrong: aspirin gives no reperfusion for a salvageable M1 occlusion, and adding an antiplatelet in a fully anticoagulated patient before reperfusion is decided raises bleeding risk.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 4 days ago. She has had asthma since childhood. She uses only a reliever inhaler and has never been prescribed a preventer. On arrival she speaks in short phrases and is using her accessory muscles. Pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, temperature 37.4 °C and SpO2 91% on room air. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. The trachea is central and air entry is equal on both sides. Over the first hour she receives oxygen by nasal prongs, salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes and oral prednisolone 50 mg. She is still alert but still speaks only in phrases. Pulse is 122/min, respiratory rate 27/min and SpO2 93% on 2 L/min oxygen. Wheeze persists. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no pneumothorax or consolidation.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This woman has acute severe asthma. She speaks only in phrases, uses her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 91% on room air. She has no features of life-threatening asthma: she is alert, with no cyanosis, no silent chest and no exhaustion. She has had an hour of optimal first-line treatment: repeated salbutamol by spacer, ipratropium, oral prednisolone and oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%. She is still in the severe category. The chest X-ray rules out a pneumothorax and consolidation. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes for severe acute asthma that has not responded to first-line bronchodilators. She should keep having frequent salbutamol, and senior and ICU staff should be told. Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment because it adds little and causes arrhythmias and vomiting. IV hydrocortisone works no better than the oral prednisolone she has already had. IV salbutamol is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond, in a critical care setting. Nebulised adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction, not acute asthma. Before discharge she will need a preventer containing an inhaled corticosteroid and a written action plan.
why: Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment for acute asthma: it adds little bronchodilation to inhaled therapy and has a narrow therapeutic index, with arrhythmias, seizures and vomiting.
She has already had oral prednisolone 50 mg and can swallow, so IV hydrocortisone gives no extra benefit and repeats her corticosteroid.

An IV salbutamol infusion is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond to other treatment, in a critical care setting; it causes more tachycardia, lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia, and she has no life-threatening features.
Nebulised adrenaline treats anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction such as croup, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, allergen exposure or stridor.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for review of heartburn. For 9 years he has had burning retrosternal pain after evening meals on most days, with sour fluid coming up into his throat when he lies down at night. He has treated it with over-the-counter antacids and has never seen a doctor about it. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years and stopped 5 years ago. He drinks about 10 standard drinks of alcohol a week. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. His BMI is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 110 cm. Abdominal examination is normal. A resting 12-lead ECG is normal. Haemoglobin is 146 g/L (reference 130–180 g/L) and ferritin is 120 µg/L (reference 30–500 µg/L).
items.ask: Which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
items.explanation: This man has had untreated gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) for 9 years, with typical burning retrosternal pain after meals and regurgitation at night. He also has most of the recognised risk factors for Barrett's oesophagus: male sex, age over 50, reflux for many years, nocturnal symptoms, central obesity and a history of smoking. In Barrett's oesophagus, repeated acid injury replaces the squamous lining of the distal oesophagus with columnar epithelium showing intestinal metaplasia. It causes no symptoms of its own, but it can progress through dysplasia to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so it is the key complication to look for and counsel about. Cancer Council Australia and eTG guidance support gastroscopy for a man over 50 with chronic reflux and several Barrett's risk factors, even without alarm features. Management alongside this is lifestyle change (weight loss, smaller and earlier evening meals, raising the head of the bed) and a standard-dose PPI. If Barrett's is found, he needs endoscopic surveillance. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking and heavy alcohol use, not reflux. Eosinophilic oesophagitis and achalasia are not complications of GORD. Distal gastric adenocarcinoma is driven by Helicobacter pylori, not reflux.
why: Wrong: squamous cell carcinoma is mainly caused by heavy smoking and alcohol use, not acid reflux, and his moderate drinking and past smoking make it much less likely than reflux-driven metaplasia.
Wrong: eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic disorder that usually affects younger atopic men with dysphagia or food bolus impaction, and it is not a complication of long-standing reflux.
Wrong: achalasia is a primary motility disorder caused by loss of myenteric neurons, and it presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids rather than developing from reflux.
Wrong: adenocarcinoma of the distal stomach is mainly linked to Helicobacter pylori and atrophic gastritis, not to acid reflux into the oesophagus.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man at a rural hospital, 3 hours from a PCI centre, has 2 hours of crushing chest pain and no bleeding history. ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF.

GTN only relieves symptoms and does not reperfuse, and in inferior STEMI it can cause severe hypotension if the right ventricle is involved.
Nothing here suggests dissection (no tearing pain to the back), and imaging would only delay time-critical reperfusion.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man is leaving the surgical ward on day 2 after laparoscopic appendicectomy with oxycodone 5 mg up to four times daily. He takes oral iron. Bowels not opened; abdomen soft.
items.explanation: Opioids predictably cause constipation, and oral iron and reduced mobility after surgery add to it, so a regular laxative should be prescribed whenever an opioid is supplied at discharge (ACSQHC 2022). eTG recommends a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative for opioid-induced constipation, usually both, such as macrogol with senna. A stool softener used alone does not counter the slowed gut movement caused by opioids, so it is not enough as prevention.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury has fixed dilated pupils and no brainstem reflexes. He received a thiopentone infusion until yesterday; serum levels remain high.
items.ask: Which test best confirms brain death?
items.explanation: High levels of a sedative like thiopentone mean the clinical brain death tests cannot be relied on. The ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation then requires imaging that shows no blood flow to the brain, such as radionuclide perfusion scintigraphy or four-vessel catheter angiography. Sedatives do not change cerebral blood flow, so these tests still work.
why: EEG measures cortical activity, which thiopentone suppresses, so it cannot separate drug effect from death, and ANZICS does not accept it.
Transcranial Doppler depends on the operator, can miss flow when the skull blocks the ultrasound, and is not accepted by ANZICS for brain death.
MRI shows structural damage, not whether blood is flowing through the brain, so it cannot confirm that all brain function has stopped.
Evoked potentials test only some sensory pathways, not the whole brain, and are not accepted for diagnosing brain death in Australia.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man collapses in the emergency department waiting area 20 minutes after triage. He had come in with 4 hours of central chest heaviness and nausea. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. His first rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. He receives CPR, three shocks, adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV. Spontaneous circulation returns after 12 minutes. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve-mask on 15 L/min oxygen. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, temperature is 35.6 °C and SpO2 is 97%. GCS is 3. A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V5. A venous blood gas taken 5 minutes after return of circulation shows: pH 7.09 (7.32 to 7.42); pCO2 62 mm Hg (41 to 51); bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22 to 28); base excess -11 mmol/L (-2 to +2); lactate 9.2 mmol/L (below 2.0); potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2); glucose 15.1 mmol/L (4.0 to 7.8).
items.ask: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base disturbance?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Acute respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
items.explanation: The pH of 7.09 shows a severe acidaemia. There are two causes, and each one lowers the pH. First, the pCO2 of 62 mm Hg is high even for a venous sample, so there is a respiratory acidosis. This comes from low cardiac output during the arrest and poor ventilation with the bag-valve-mask. Second, the bicarbonate of 18 mmol/L, base excess of -11 and lactate of 9.2 mmol/L show a lactic metabolic acidosis from 12 minutes of low tissue perfusion. If the lungs were compensating for the metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula (1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35 +/- 2 mm Hg) says the pCO2 should be low. Instead it is high, so a second, respiratory process is present. This matters for his care. ANZCOR post-resuscitation guidance asks for normocapnia, so his ventilation should be increased and adjusted to arterial gases. Do not give bicarbonate routinely. items.stem: A 78-year-old woman sees her general practitioner about a painful ulcer on the tip of her left second toe. It has not healed in 2 months. The left foot is cool and hairless, and the pedal pulses cannot be felt. The ulcer is 0.8 cm across, dry and punched out, with a pale base and no surrounding erythema. Probe to bone is negative. Monofilament sensation is reduced at 2 of 10 sites. eGFR is 41 mL/min/1.73 m2. Handheld Doppler studies show: right brachial systolic 146 mmHg, left brachial systolic 140 mmHg; left dorsalis pedis systolic 178 mmHg and left posterior tibial systolic 184 mmHg (ABI 1.26); left pedal waveforms monophasic; left hallux systolic 22 mmHg (toe-brachial index 0.15; normal above 0.70).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the vascular studies?

The digital arteries are usually spared from calcification, so the toe pressure shows the true perfusion of the foot. A toe pressure below 30 mmHg means severe ischaemia and a low chance of healing. With rest pain and tissue loss, this is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, which needs urgent vascular imaging and referral for revascularisation. Wrong: a toe pressure below 30 mmHg predicts poor healing and, with rest pain and tissue loss, means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia that needs urgent vascular referral.

Total bilirubin 24 µmol/L (<20)
ALP 440 U/L (30-110)
GGT 210 U/L (<40)

Ultrasound shows a gallbladder wall thickened to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. The common bile duct measures 5 mm, but bowel gas hides its distal end. She is given analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics, and is admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

items.stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen right knee that came on suddenly overnight. Two years ago he had an attack in his left big toe that settled on its own. He has hypertension and stage 4 chronic kidney disease. He takes amlodipine, irbesartan and furosemide, and has no drug allergies. He recalls no injury. His temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 88/min and blood pressure 148/86 mm Hg. The right knee is hot, red and tensely swollen with a large effusion, and the skin is intact. Investigations show:
Serum creatinine 245 µmol/L (60–110)
eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m² (>90)
Serum urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.20–0.42)
CRP 64 mg/L (<5)
Synovial fluid: white cell count 22 000 ×10^6/L with 80% neutrophils; needle-shaped, negatively birefringent intracellular crystals; Gram stain shows no organisms; culture pending.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this attack?
items.explanation: The aspirate shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, so this is an acute flare of gout. He is afebrile with a negative Gram stain. An NSAID, low-dose colchicine and a corticosteroid work about equally well for a flare, so the choice depends on comorbidities. This man has severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR 23) and takes an angiotensin receptor blocker and a loop diuretic. That makes an NSAID unsafe, and colchicine can build up to toxic levels. A short course of oral prednisolone (eTG) is the safest effective option. Intra-articular corticosteroid is another option, but only once infection is reasonably excluded, and the culture is still pending. Culture must be followed to its final report, because crystals do not rule out coexisting infection. Allopurinol is not used to treat the attack itself. Antibiotics are not indicated when the patient is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present.
why: Allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy for long-term prevention; it does not treat a flare and is started later, at a low dose for his eGFR, with flare prophylaxis.
Colchicine is cleared by the kidneys and builds up in severe chronic kidney disease, causing toxicity such as diarrhoea, myopathy and bone marrow suppression, so a corticosteroid is the safer choice.
An NSAID given with an angiotensin receptor blocker and a diuretic (the 'triple whammy') in someone with an eGFR of 23 risks acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

Empirical antibiotics for septic arthritis are not needed: he is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial white cell count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present, though the culture should still be followed up.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has 4 months of thirst and nocturia. BMI is 36 kg/m2 with acanthosis nigricans. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, specific gravity 1.022.
items.ask: Which test best confirms the diagnosis?

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, which gives dilute urine without glucose, not concentrated urine with glucosuria.
GAD antibodies help tell autoimmune from type 2 diabetes once diabetes is confirmed, but they do not diagnose diabetes itself.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the body still makes, which helps classify diabetes after diagnosis, but it does not confirm hyperglycaemia.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and yellow eyes. Today his wife noticed he was muddled. He has untreated gallstones and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. On arrival he is jaundiced and disoriented to time. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on room air. The right upper quadrant is tender. Results: total bilirubin 104 µmol/L (reference <20), conjugated bilirubin 82 µmol/L, ALP 438 U/L (30–110), GGT 590 U/L (<50), ALT 112 U/L (<40), lipase 52 U/L (<60), white cell count 19.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 139 µmol/L (60–110), INR 1.2 and venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows gallbladder calculi with a 3 mm wall and a common bile duct of 12 mm containing a distal shadowing calculus. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given IV amoxicillin, IV gentamicin and 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. His blood pressure is now 98/60 mm Hg.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This man has Reynolds' pentad: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension. Under the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 this is severe (grade III) acute cholangitis, because he has neurological and cardiovascular dysfunction. It is caused by a stone in a dilated common bile duct, with a cholestatic liver test pattern, and he also has sepsis with hypoperfusion (lactate 3.8 mmol/L and acute kidney injury). The eTG and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard say to take blood cultures, give IV antibiotics within 60 minutes (amoxicillin plus gentamicin for biliary sepsis) and give fluids, all of which has been done. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a blocked duct. Once he has been resuscitated, he needs urgent source control by decompressing the bile duct with ERCP (sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or a stent if he is too unstable), and his care should be escalated to ICU. Cholecystectomy should follow once he has recovered, ideally during the same admission. A normal lipase and a thin gallbladder wall make gallstone pancreatitis and acute cholecystitis unlikely.
why: Wrong: cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the stone blocking the common bile duct, and operating on a septic, hypotensive patient is high risk. It is planned after the duct has been cleared and he has recovered.
Wrong: ultrasound has already shown a dilated duct with a stone in it, so MRCP would only delay drainage in a deteriorating septic patient.

Wrong: cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the blocked common bile duct. It is used for acute cholecystitis in unfit patients, whereas percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is the fallback if ERCP fails.
Wrong: delaying drainage by 72 hours is acceptable only in mild cholangitis that responds to antibiotics. In severe cholangitis with hypotension and confusion, this delay increases the risk of death.

items.stem: A 67-year-old retired electrician is reviewed on day 3 of admission to the general surgical ward. He came in with 2 days of constant left iliac fossa pain, loose stools and a temperature of 38.4 °C. On admission, CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed multiple sigmoid diverticula and a 5 cm segment of sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding. There was no abscess, extraluminal gas, fistula or obstruction. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, fluids and paracetamol. He is now afebrile, eating normally and has minimal pain, and he has been switched to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He has never had any lower bowel investigation and did not return his last two national bowel screening kits. There is no family history of bowel disease. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 72/min and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding. Haemoglobin is 141 g/L (130–180), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0) and CRP 34 mg/L (<5). He is to be discharged today.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up investigation?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis in 48 hours
items.explanation: This man has CT-confirmed acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis and is getting better on treatment. He is 67, has never had his colon examined and has not done his bowel screening, so cancer in the thickened segment has to be excluded. Colonoscopy should be done once the inflammation has settled, usually about 6 weeks after recovery. CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy are alternatives if colonoscopy is unsuitable. Scoping during acute inflammation is avoided because inflating the bowel with air and passing the scope through the inflamed segment risks perforation. A repeat CT is only needed if he fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse. Tumour markers such as CEA are not used to diagnose or screen for colorectal cancer. A faecal immunochemical test is a screening tool for people without symptoms. It cannot replace looking directly at a segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.

Colonoscopy during or just after acute diverticulitis risks perforating the inflamed colon and is harder to interpret while the inflammation persists, so it should be delayed.
CEA is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose or exclude colorectal cancer and is used only to monitor known disease.
A faecal immunochemical test is a screening test for people without symptoms and cannot exclude cancer in a sigmoid segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.

items.stem:
A 29-year-old woman who is a primary school teacher comes to her general practitioner with a 5-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain and loose stools. She opens her bowels three to four times a day, mostly in the morning, with urgency, and the pain eases after defecation. She is bloated most afternoons. She has had no rectal bleeding or weight loss, and she does not wake at night to open her bowels. She has not travelled overseas. No family members have bowel disease. She takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 76/min, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg and BMI 23 kg/m2. The abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no masses. Rectal examination is normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115–165)
Ferritin 62 µg/L (30–300)
C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5)
Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0)
Tissue transglutaminase IgA 1 U/mL (<7)
Stool microscopy, culture and PCR: no pathogens detected
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This young woman has symptoms that fit irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. She has recurrent lower abdominal pain that eases after defecation, a change in stool frequency and form, and bloating. She has no red flags: no rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, mass or family history. Her full blood count, ferritin and CRP are normal. Coeliac serology is negative and valid, because her total IgA is normal. Stool tests show no infection. The main serious condition left to exclude is inflammatory bowel disease, because loose stools with urgency in a young adult can be early Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and a normal CRP does not rule it out. The first-line test before making a positive diagnosis of IBS is faecal calprotectin, as recommended in eTG and Australian gastroenterology practice. It is cheap and non-invasive. A result below 50 µg/g makes IBD unlikely and avoids colonoscopy. A raised result calls for gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is wrong at this stage because it is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin. Duodenal biopsy is wrong because a negative tTG-IgA with normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely. A lactose hydrogen breath test is wrong because it does not exclude IBD, and a trial of cutting out dairy is the preferred first step. A faecal immunochemical test is wrong because in Australia it is a screening test for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms, not a way to assess a symptomatic young adult.
why: Colonoscopy is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin, neither of which she has yet.
Duodenal biopsy is not needed because a negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
A lactose hydrogen breath test cannot exclude inflammatory bowel disease, and a trial of avoiding dairy is preferred over formal breath testing.
A faecal immunochemical test is a population screening tool for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms and is not used to investigate symptomatic young adults in Australia.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman, a retired pharmacist, sees her general practitioner with 8 days of cough. The cough began after a coryzal illness and is now productive of rust-coloured sputum, with fevers and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. She has never smoked and has no drug allergies. Temperature is 38.4 °C, pulse 102/min, respiratory rate 24/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg and SpO2 95% on room air. She is alert and oriented, with an abbreviated mental test score of 10/10. There is dullness, bronchial breathing and crackles at the right base. Urgent blood results are: white cell count 15.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 12.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 74 µmol/L (45-90), sodium 135 mmol/L (135-145) and C-reactive protein 162 mg/L (less than 5). A chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
items.ask: Which of the following is this patient's CURB-65 score?
items.explanation: CURB-65 gives one point for each of five criteria: new confusion; urea above 7 mmol/L; respiratory rate of 30/min or more; systolic BP below 90 mmHg or diastolic BP of 60 mmHg or less; and age 65 years or older. This patient meets none of them. She is alert with an AMTS of 10/10. Her urea of 6.8 mmol/L is below the CURB-65 cut-off of 7, even though it sits near the top of the laboratory range. Her respiratory rate of 24/min is high, but below 30. Her BP of 112/68 mmHg is above both thresholds. At 64, she is just under the age criterion. Her score is 0, which means low-severity pneumonia. In a stable patient with SpO2 of 92% or more, this supports oral treatment at home. eTG recommends amoxicillin 1 g 8-hourly for 5 days, with review at 48 hours and a safety-net plan. Clinical judgement still applies alongside the score. Tachycardia, neutrophilia and a high CRP show a systemic inflammatory response, but they are not CURB-65 criteria.
why: A score of 1 would need one criterion. Students reach it by scoring her respiratory rate of 24/min (the cut-off is 30 or more) or by counting her age of 64 as 65 or older.

A score of 2 would need two criteria. Students reach it by wrongly scoring the urea of 6.8 mmol/L (the cut-off is above 7) and the raised respiratory rate, or by counting the tachycardia, which is not part of CURB-65.
A score of 3 would mean high-severity pneumonia needing hospital admission. This woman is alert, normotensive, younger than 65 and has a urea below 7 mmol/L.
A score of 4 would need four criteria such as confusion and hypotension, and she has none of them. The high white cell count and CRP do not count towards the score.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man comes to his general practitioner with 3 weeks of sharp anal pain. It starts with each bowel motion and lasts about 2 hours afterwards, and there is a small amount of bright red blood on the toilet paper. The pain began after a week of hard stools while he was driving long-haul freight. For the past 2 weeks he has taken psyllium daily, increased his fluid intake, used warm sitz baths and applied lidocaine gel. His stools are now soft, but the pain has improved only slightly. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and erectile dysfunction treated with tadalafil 5 mg daily. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 134/82 mmHg. With a chaperone present, inspection shows a single linear tear in the posterior midline of the anal margin with clean, soft edges. There is no sentinel tag, induration or swelling. He is too tender for a digital rectal examination, so it is not done.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% applied to the anal margin
Diltiazem 2% applied to the anal margin
Hydrocortisone with cinchocaine applied to the anal margin
Botulinum toxin injected into the internal sphincter
items.explanation: This man has an acute primary anal fissure. The fissure is in the posterior midline, has soft edges and no sentinel tag, and has been present for less than 6 weeks. The pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter, which reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm and stops the tear healing. His stools are now soft, but he is still in pain after 2 weeks of conservative care, so the eTG recommends adding a topical drug that relaxes the sphincter. The two choices are glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% and diltiazem 2%. GTN is contraindicated in anyone taking a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. He takes tadalafil daily, and its long half-life means simply skipping doses would not make GTN safe. Topical diltiazem 2% twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks heals about as many fissures as GTN and causes fewer headaches. He should keep using fibre, fluids and sitz baths. If the fissure becomes chronic, he should be referred to a surgeon. Any bleeding that continues after the fissure heals needs investigation.

Codeine causes constipation, and hard stools would reopen the fissure and keep the pain and spasm going, so it should be avoided.
A topical corticosteroid with local anaesthetic does not relax the sphincter and does not speed fissure healing, and long-term use thins the perianal skin.

Botulinum toxin is a specialist second-line treatment for chronic fissures, or for fissures that have not responded to topical sphincter relaxants, so it is not the next step for an acute fissure that has not yet been treated with one.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a dilatation and curettage for heavy menstrual bleeding. The scrub nurse notes yellow fatty tissue in the curettings. Afterwards she is stable with mild lower abdominal pain.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after sudden, severe, tearing chest pain that radiated between her shoulder blades while she was gardening. She fainted briefly when the pain began. She has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her medicines are perindopril and amlodipine. On arrival, her blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg in the left arm and 136/80 mmHg in the right arm, pulse is 104/min and SpO2 is 96% on room air. An early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal edge. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that starts just above the aortic valve and extends into the descending thoracic aorta, with a moderate high-attenuation pericardial effusion. Twenty minutes later she becomes pale and confused. Her blood pressure is 82/54 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, jugular venous pressure is raised 6 cm and her heart sounds are muffled. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and crossmatched blood is available.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate open repair in the operating theatre
items.explanation: This woman has an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, because the flap starts in the ascending aorta. She now has the complication most likely to kill her: cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardium. The high-attenuation (blood-density) pericardial effusion, low blood pressure, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and confusion are the Beck triad with shock. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency. When it is complicated by haemopericardium and shock, the 2024 ESC guidelines and the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidance used in Australia say she should go straight to theatre for open replacement of the ascending aorta, with blood products given while she is moved. Draining the pericardium only fixes the tamponade, and the blood pressure it restores can make the aorta bleed again. Lowering the heart rate or blood pressure is wrong while she is hypotensive. Anticoagulants make the bleeding worse.

Percutaneous pericardiocentesis raises the blood pressure, which can restart bleeding from the aorta into the pericardium, so it is kept for controlled, small-volume drainage only when theatre cannot be reached in time.
Endovascular stent-graft repair is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection and cannot treat a tear in the ascending aorta just above the valve that is bleeding into the pericardium.
Heparin speeds up bleeding into the pericardium and the false lumen; giving antithrombotics because of the low-grade suspicion of a coronary syndrome is a known harmful error in dissection.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man walks into his general practice without an appointment. He has had chest discomfort for 40 minutes. It began while he was gardening and has not eased with rest. He describes a heavy band across his chest that spreads to his neck and both shoulders, and he feels nauseated and clammy. For the past 2 weeks he has had similar but brief tightness when walking uphill, which settled within minutes of stopping. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and takes metformin and perindopril. He smoked for 35 years and stopped 2 years ago. He is pale and sweaty. Temperature is 36.6°C, pulse 92/min and regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The heart sounds are dual with no murmur, and the chest is clear. Both calves are soft and non-tender.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This man has ongoing ischaemic-type chest pain at rest. The pain is heavy, spreads to the neck and shoulders, and comes with nausea and sweating. Australian guidelines (National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guidelines, eTG Cardiovascular, and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard) say a 12-lead ECG should be recorded and read within 10 minutes of first medical contact. It is the single test that sorts the patient into the right pathway straight away. New ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (or LBBB with ongoing symptoms) means STEMI. In that case, call 000 for ambulance transfer for primary PCI or fibrinolysis, and do not wait for any blood result. If the ECG does not show STEMI, the patient still needs urgent transfer for serial troponins. Equal arm pressures, no aortic regurgitation murmur, normal oxygen saturation and normal calves make aortic dissection and PE less likely, so the ECG comes first. Troponin takes time to rise, and a negative early result cannot rule out infarction, so it must not delay reperfusion. A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would hold up transfer. A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected PE, and this history does not suggest PE. CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain, not for ongoing pain at rest.
why: Troponin may still be normal early in infarction and must never delay reperfusion, so it comes after the ECG and should not hold up transfer.
A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would delay the test that decides immediate management.
A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected pulmonary embolism, and this man has ischaemic-type pain with no PE risk factors, normal SpO2 and normal calves.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain and is not appropriate for ongoing ischaemic pain at rest.

items.stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness when climbing stairs at the café she manages. Her cycles are regular every 28 days. Over the past year her periods have lengthened to 7 days. On heavy days she changes a super pad every 2 hours, floods overnight and passes large clots. She has no bruising, nosebleeds or change in bowel habit. She and her partner stopped using condoms 2 months ago and hope to conceive within the next year. Her only medicine is folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg, pulse 98/min and temperature 36.7 °C. She has conjunctival pallor. Abdominal, speculum and bimanual examinations are normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165)
MCV 71 fL (80–100)
Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150–400)
Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300)
CRP 3 mg/L (<5)
TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Urine β-hCG negative
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral iron and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Oral iron and the combined oral contraceptive pill
Intravenous iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and referral for diagnostic hysteroscopy
items.explanation: She has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, reactive thrombocytosis, ferritin 5 µg/L with a normal CRP) caused by heavy menstrual bleeding. Management must replace the deficit and treat the cause. Under eTG and the National Blood Authority guidance, oral iron is first line in a stable patient who has not yet tried it. Daily or alternate-day dosing works, and alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and tolerance. Recheck the FBC in 2 to 4 weeks (expect a rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks) and continue for about 3 months after the Hb normalises. The levonorgestrel IUD is usually first line for heavy menstrual bleeding (ACSQHC Clinical Care Standard), but it and the combined pill both prevent pregnancy, and she is trying to conceive. Tranexamic acid (1 g orally three to four times daily for up to 5 days during heavy bleeding) is a non-hormonal option. It reduces menstrual loss by about 40 to 50%, is taken only while bleeding and does not affect fertility. She has a normal pelvic examination and no risk factors for endometrial pathology, so invasive investigation is not needed yet. B: the LNG-IUD is contraceptive and does not suit a woman trying to conceive. C: the combined pill prevents ovulation and conception, so it goes against her plan for pregnancy. D: IV iron is for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and none of these applies. E: hysteroscopy is for women aged 45 or older, those with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, or those whose medical treatment has failed.
why: Wrong: the levonorgestrel IUD is contraceptive, so it conflicts with her wish to conceive, even though it is often first line for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Wrong: the combined oral contraceptive pill suppresses ovulation and prevents the pregnancy she is trying for.
Wrong: intravenous iron is reserved for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and she is stable and has not tried oral iron.
Wrong: hysteroscopy is not indicated in a 24-year-old with a normal pelvic examination, no endometrial risk factors and no failed medical treatment.
