items.stem: A 72-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with a racing heart and mild central chest tightness. Both started suddenly 70 minutes ago while she was watching television. She has never had this before. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her pulse is 138/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.7 °C. Her chest is clear and she has no peripheral oedema. A 12-lead ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 140/min, a narrow QRS and no ST-segment or T-wave change. Blood was taken on arrival, 75 minutes after symptom onset: high-sensitivity troponin T 9 ng/L (99th centile 14), creatinine 84 µmol/L (eGFR 66 mL/min/1.73 m^2), potassium 4.4 mmol/L and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of her troponin result?
options: Myocardial infarction cannot yet be ruled out at this point
Acute myocardial infarction is excluded by this single value
Rate-related type 2 myocardial infarction is confirmed
Chronic myocardial injury from renal impairment is shown
Unstable angina is excluded by this normal value
items.explanation: Her high-sensitivity troponin T of 9 ng/L is below the 99th centile, but it was taken only 75 minutes after her symptoms began. Troponin takes time to rise after myocardial injury, so one value taken this soon can miss an evolving infarction. The NHFA/CSANZ ACS guideline accepts a single-sample rule-out only when the hs-troponin T is very low (below about 5 ng/L) and symptoms started more than 3 hours before the sample. Otherwise, the test is repeated using an accelerated protocol (usually at 2 hours, or at 1 hour with validated algorithms) and the change between the two values is assessed. Her chest tightness, age, hypertension and diabetes make ACS an important alternative cause and a possible trigger for her AF. So this result does not yet rule out myocardial infarction, and she needs a repeat troponin while her AF is rate-controlled. A: A value below the 99th centile does not rule out infarction when it is taken less than 3 hours after onset and is above the very-low threshold. C: A type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal. D: Chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her eGFR of 66 does not explain any rise. E: Troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.
why: Correct: a single hs-troponin T below the 99th centile but above the very-low rule-out level, taken under 3 hours after onset, cannot rule out infarction, so a repeat is needed.
Wrong: a type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal.
Wrong: chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her near-normal renal function does not explain any rise.
Wrong: troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.

items.stem:
A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, distension and repeated vomiting, which is now faeculent. She has passed no flatus for 24 hours. She has known gallstones and has never had abdominal surgery. Her medicines are perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 108/min, blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and respiratory rate is 16/min. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her abdomen is distended, with high-pitched bowel sounds and no peritonism. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels. Venous blood results:
pH 7.43 (7.32 to 7.42)
pCO2 46 mmHg (41 to 51)
Bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22 to 28)
Base excess +6 mmol/L (-2 to +2)
Lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
Sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145)
Potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2)
Chloride 93 mmol/L (95 to 110)
Creatinine 128 µmol/L (her baseline is 78)
items.ask: Which of the following best describes these blood gas findings?
options: Respiratory acidosis with renal bicarbonate retention
Lactic acidosis from metformin and kidney injury
Normal anion gap acidosis from small bowel losses
Metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid and volume loss
Mixed high anion gap acidosis and alkalosis
items.explanation: The pH is at the alkalaemic end, and bicarbonate (30 mmol/L) and base excess (+6) are both raised. That means the main problem is metabolic alkalosis. The low chloride (93 mmol/L) and low potassium (2.8 mmol/L) show it is hypochloraemic and hypokalaemic, the typical picture with vomiting. Losing gastric hydrochloric acid produces the alkalosis. Losing volume then keeps it going: it causes a prerenal acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.6 times her baseline) and switches on aldosterone, so the kidney holds on to bicarbonate and loses potassium. A venous pCO2 of 46 mmHg is within the normal range and fits mild respiratory compensation, not a primary respiratory problem. The anion gap is normal (136 - (93 + 30) = 13) and lactate is normal, so there is no hidden acidosis, although a normal lactate does not rule out bowel ischaemia. In practice she needs IV 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride, magnesium checked, and her perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen withheld.
why: Wrong: a primary respiratory acidosis needs an acidaemic pH and a raised pCO2, but her pH is high and her venous pCO2 is normal, so the raised bicarbonate is the primary change.
Wrong: metformin and the kidney injury make this a tempting choice, but her lactate (1.8 mmol/L), anion gap (13) and pH are all normal, so there is no lactic acidosis.
Wrong: losing alkaline small bowel fluid can cause a normal anion gap acidosis, but her bicarbonate is raised and her pH is not acidaemic.
Wrong: with a normal anion gap of 13 and a normal lactate, there is no evidence of a second, high anion gap acidosis alongside the alkalosis.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man diagnosed with HIV 8 months ago has had an undetectable viral load for 6 months on dolutegravir plus tenofovir-emtricitabine. He feels well and asks to stop treatment.
items.explanation: ART suppresses HIV but does not cure it. Latent virus persists in reservoirs such as resting memory CD4 cells, so viral load usually rebounds within weeks of stopping. CD4 counts fall over months to years after stopping, so rebound viraemia comes well before any AIDS-defining illness.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has an excisional biopsy of a changing pigmented lesion on his back. Histopathology shows superficial spreading melanoma, Breslow thickness 1.6 mm, without ulceration. His regional nodes are impalpable.
items.ask: Most appropriate addition to wide excision?

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites vomits 400 mL of fresh blood. His pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Endoscopy is being arranged.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 3 days of tingling that started in her feet and has spread up to her waist. Eighteen months ago she had 2 weeks of blurred vision and pain on moving her left eye, which got better without treatment. She takes no medicines. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 80 beats/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Cranial nerve and upper limb examination is normal. Tone is increased in both legs. Hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion are 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk, and both plantar responses are extensor. Pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. A bladder scan shows 900 mL. Full blood count and C-reactive protein are normal.

options: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
Nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs
Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine only
Urgent gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the whole spine

items.stem: A 44-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward at 08:00. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is tender at McBurney's point with localised guarding, and there is no generalised rigidity. White cell count is 14.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), neutrophils 11.6 x10^9/L (2.0–7.5), CRP 52 mg/L (<5) and creatinine 80 µmol/L (60–110). Wrong: treating with antibiotics alone at home is an alternative only after a shared decision, and about 3 in 10 patients still need an appendicectomy within a year; he is booked for and agreeable to surgery, the standard treatment.

items.stem: A 20-hour-old girl is reviewed on the postnatal ward because the midwife reports that she has stopped feeding and started grunting. Her mother carried group B streptococcus and received intravenous benzylpenicillin 90 minutes before the birth. The membranes had ruptured 22 hours before delivery, and the mother's temperature in labour was 38.4 °C. On examination, the baby is lethargic and mottled. Temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 184/min, respirations 72/min, systolic pressure 55 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. She has subcostal recession and grunting. Heart sounds are normal and the femoral pulses are palpable. Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L. Intravenous access has been obtained, and antibiotics are about to be given.

A positive blood culture is the reference standard for confirming early-onset sepsis. It identifies the organism (most often GBS or E. coli) and its antibiotic sensitivities. Under the RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines and Queensland Clinical Guidelines, at least 1 mL is taken before the first doses of benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, but antibiotics are not delayed to get it. Early-onset sepsis comes from maternal flora at birth, not from the urinary tract, so urine culture is not recommended in the first 72 hours and would rarely be positive.
A chest X-ray may show pneumonia, but GBS pneumonia can look the same as surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea, and the film cannot identify an organism.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser sees her general practitioner with 10 weeks of right neck pain. The pain runs down the back of her arm to her middle finger and is worse when she looks up. Eight weeks ago she started regular paracetamol and ibuprofen and a supervised physiotherapy program. The pain has eased only a little, and she still drops her hair dryer. She has no hand clumsiness, change in gait or bladder symptoms. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 74/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. Right elbow extension and wrist flexion are 4-/5, the same as 8 weeks ago, and the right triceps reflex is reduced. Sensation is reduced over the right middle finger. Tone, coordination and the lower limb examination are normal, and Hoffmann's sign is absent. MRI of the neck shows severe right C6-7 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C7 nerve root, with a normal cord.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day transfer to an emergency department
Outpatient referral to a spine surgeon
items.explanation: This is a right C7 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis. The radicular pain runs to the middle finger and gets worse on neck extension. There is weakness of elbow extension and wrist flexion, a reduced triceps reflex and C7 sensory loss, and the MRI shows concordant C6-7 foraminal stenosis. That combination warrants referral to a spine surgeon to assess her for decompression. Urgent assessment is not needed: there are no myelopathic symptoms, no upper motor neuron signs, her weakness is not getting worse and the cord is normal. items.stem: A 63-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with 6 days of worsening breathlessness and a cough that now brings up more green sputum than usual. His JVP is not raised and he has no ankle oedema. A 12-lead ECG shows a regular rhythm at 112/min, with an upright P wave of the same shape before every QRS complex in lead II. The PR interval is 160 ms, QRS 90 ms and axis +60°. There are no ST-segment or T-wave changes, and V1 has a dominant S wave. items.stem: A 69-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 24 hours of crampy, diffuse abdominal pain, profuse watery diarrhoea without blood, and repeated vomiting. Pure-tone audiometry thresholds (dB HL; normal 20 or less) are:
Right air conduction: 250 Hz 35, 500 Hz 40, 1 kHz 45, 2 kHz 55, 4 kHz 60

Left air and bone conduction: 10 to 15 at every frequency

The masked bone conduction thresholds are raised by the same amount, never more than 5 dB from air conduction. items.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 10 weeks of crampy right lower abdominal pain and four to six loose stools a day. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (130–180), CRP 42 mg/L (<5) and albumin 31 g/L (35–50). Faecal calprotectin is 640 µg/g (<50). items.stem: A 21-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents on the advice of their general practitioner because of jaundice. The liver is firm, 3 cm below the right costal margin. There is no bruising and no petechiae. options: Phytomenadione 1 mg by slow intravenous injection

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with breathlessness and wheeze that began 6 hours ago, two days into a head cold. She has had asthma since childhood and uses only a salbutamol reliever. When she arrived 70 minutes ago, she could speak only in phrases and was using her accessory muscles. Since then she has had salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for three doses, prednisolone 50 mg orally, and oxygen by nasal prongs. She is alert but still speaks in phrases and uses her accessory muscles. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 118/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. There is widespread expiratory wheeze with equal air entry on both sides, and no rash or lip swelling. Venous blood gas: pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg (reference 41–51), lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Salbutamol is being continued.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This is severe acute asthma (she speaks only in phrases and uses her accessory muscles) that has not responded well to an hour of standard treatment. She has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium by spacer, oral prednisolone within the first hour, and oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 92–96%. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise adding IV magnesium sulfate (10 mmol over 20 minutes in adults) for severe or life-threatening asthma that responds poorly to the first bronchodilators. Salbutamol continues alongside it. She has no life-threatening features: she is alert, her SpO2 is 90% or above, her pCO2 is low rather than normal or rising, and her chest is not silent. So she does not yet need intubation, but she needs senior review and close monitoring. Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines because it adds little to standard treatment and causes arrhythmias, vomiting and seizures. IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or impending arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. IV hydrocortisone adds nothing when oral prednisolone has been given and can be swallowed. Antibiotics are not indicated, because the trigger is viral and there is no consolidation.

IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or near-arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, stridor or hypotension.
She has already had oral prednisolone and can swallow; IV corticosteroid is no more effective and is only needed when oral intake is not possible.
A viral cold triggered this attack, and with no fever, purulent sputum or consolidation there is no indication for antibiotics.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because she has not opened her bowels for 6 days. Nine days ago she had an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. She had to strain, passing them caused sharp anal pain, and there was bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is passing flatus and has no vomiting or abdominal pain. She takes ferrous sulfate for iron deficiency. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 120/78 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and bowel sounds are normal. Anal inspection shows a posterior midline fissure. Digital rectal examination finds hard stool and no mass. Haemoglobin is 124 g/L (115–165), ferritin 20 µg/L (30–300), corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10–2.60) and TSH 1.4 mIU/L (0.5–4.0). The opioid will be weaned and simple analgesia started.

Serum creatinine is 164 µmol/L (72 µmol/L on admission; reference 45–90), urea 11.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.6 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop the antiviral and start oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily
Stop the antiviral and start intravenous foscarnet
Continue the current regimen and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a temporary vascular catheter
Start isotonic crystalloid and reduce antiviral dosing to match renal function
items.explanation: This patient has acute kidney injury from aciclovir crystal nephropathy. Her intake is poor, her drip has been stopped, she is oliguric with dry mucous membranes, her creatinine has more than doubled and her urine shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. IV therapy should continue for the full course, at least 14 to 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, because stopping or under-treating HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. why: Wrong: oral valaciclovir is not recommended for acute HSV encephalitis while the patient is drowsy and still in the IV phase, and it is converted to aciclovir, so it would not prevent crystal formation.
Wrong: foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV and is more nephrotoxic, so it would make her kidney injury worse.
Wrong: furosemide would deepen her volume depletion and does nothing to clear crystals, and keeping full-dose aciclovir at this clearance would cause further accumulation and toxicity.
Wrong: she has no indication for urgent dialysis (no hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications), and this injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment.

items.stem: A newborn boy is assessed in the birth suite 10 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks' gestation. He weighs 3.6 kg. In the final 8 minutes of the second stage, the cardiotocograph showed a fetal heart rate of about 70/min. At birth he was floppy and apnoeic with a heart rate of 70/min. Mask ventilation in air gave no chest rise until his head was repositioned. Once his chest was rising, his heart rate reached 140/min by 3 minutes. Apgar scores were 1 at 1 minute and 7 at 5 minutes. His mother used nitrous oxide only. Her group B streptococcus screen was negative, membranes ruptured 4 hours before birth and the liquor was clear. He is now breathing on his own and crying. Temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate is 145/min, respirations are 50/min and preductal SpO2 is 88% in room air. He lies in a flexed posture with normal tone and a strong suck. The placenta was delivered 5 minutes ago and is still in the room.
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected cause of his condition at birth?

Paired umbilical arterial and venous blood gas
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
items.explanation:

A valid pair has the artery showing a lower pH and a higher pCO2 than the vein. The arterial pH, base excess and lactate measure the acidaemia. They also show whether the baby meets the hypoxia criterion for therapeutic hypothermia (pH 7.0 or less, or a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more, in the first hour). That matters because cooling works best if started within 6 hours. The placenta is still in the room, so the cord can be sampled now.

Blood culture and CRP: sepsis is unlikely here. GBS was negative, membranes ruptured only 4 hours before birth, there was no maternal fever and the liquor was clear. CRP is also unreliable this early after birth.

aEEG: this monitors babies who already have encephalopathy. This baby has normal tone, cries and sucks well.

MRI brain: this assesses the extent of HIE injury, usually around days 4 to 7. It does not confirm perinatal hypoxia at birth.

Cranial ultrasound: this is mainly a screen for intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm babies. It is insensitive for early hypoxic injury at term.
why: Sepsis is unlikely with a negative GBS screen, membranes ruptured only 4 hours before birth and clear liquor, and CRP is unreliable in the first hours of life.
aEEG is for monitoring a baby who already shows moderate to severe encephalopathy, and this baby has normal tone, a strong suck and cries.
MRI shows the pattern of HIE injury days after birth but cannot confirm the hypoxic event in the first hour.
Cranial ultrasound mainly screens preterm babies for intraventricular haemorrhage and is insensitive for early hypoxic injury in a term baby.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease and started a gluten-free diet three weeks ago. Intensely itchy, grouped, excoriated vesicles on both elbows are disturbing his sleep. G6PD activity is normal.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman has had 18 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain and fever. Ultrasound shows acute calculous cholecystitis with a 4 mm common bile duct. Bilirubin 15 µmol/L, ALP 130 U/L.

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 11 pm by his mother with noisy breathing. He was given nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (5 mL undiluted) and oral dexamethasone 7.2 mg (0.6 mg/kg), with oxygen held near his face. Sixty minutes later he is sitting on his mother's lap and playing. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 132/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and SpO2 97% in room air. He has an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest and no chest wall recession. Give a second nebulised adrenaline treatment before discharge

items.stem:
A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a general practice. He has had 14 hours of worsening generalised headache, fever and photophobia. Five days ago he came back from a week in a crowded backpacker hostel. The general practitioner gave benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intramuscularly 4 hours ago, before transfer. He takes no medicines, and his vaccination history is unknown. His temperature is 38.8 °C, pulse 116/min, respirations 22/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented (GCS 15). He has neck stiffness, with no focal neurological signs, papilloedema or rash. Two sets of blood cultures were taken on arrival. Lumbar puncture fluid analysis shows:
Appearance: turbid
Neutrophils: 2900 x10^6/L (reference 0)
Lymphocytes: 40 x10^6/L (reference less than 5)
Protein: 1.3 g/L (reference 0.15 to 0.45)
Glucose: 1.1 mmol/L (paired serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L)
Gram stain: neutrophils seen, no organisms seen
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to identify the causative organism?
options: Bacterial culture of the CSF sample
Bacterial PCR on the CSF sample
Repeat blood cultures from two sites
Viral PCR panel on the CSF sample
items.explanation: This young adult has fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness after crowded living. His lumbar puncture fluid shows a marked neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, high protein and a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of about 0.2 (below 0.4). These findings mean bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal. He correctly had parenteral benzylpenicillin in general practice before transfer. However, that dose sterilises the CSF and blood within hours, which explains why the Gram stain shows no organisms and why culture yield will be low. Nucleic acid testing (PCR) for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae on the CSF does not need live bacteria. It stays positive for days after antibiotics have started. eTG and the CDNA invasive meningococcal disease guidelines recommend it, and it is the test most likely to confirm the organism (and give the serogroup for public health) in a pretreated patient. Culture of the CSF should still be sent, because it gives antibiotic susceptibilities, but it is less likely to grow anything. Repeat blood cultures taken even later after antibiotics will give an even lower yield. A throat swab shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, so it cannot confirm invasive disease. A viral PCR panel does not fit the bacterial CSF picture.

Blood cultures taken even longer after the antibiotic dose are less likely to grow anything than the sets already taken on arrival.
A positive throat culture shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, which is common in young adults, so it supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm invasive disease.
A neutrophilic CSF with high protein and a glucose ratio below 0.4 points to a bacterial cause, not a viral one, so a viral panel will not identify this organism.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe pneumonia is drowsy and tiring. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.12, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, lactate 6 mmol/L.

This means he is tiring and heading towards respiratory failure, so he needs urgent ventilatory support.

In a pure acute respiratory acidosis the HCO3 would rise slightly to about 26 mmol/L, not fall to 16 mmol/L, and the lactate would not be high.
Chronic respiratory acidosis gives a clearly raised HCO3 from renal compensation, but here the HCO3 is low.
A respiratory alkalosis would need a PaCO2 below the predicted 30-34 mmHg, but here the PaCO2 is raised.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man on apixaban hit his head in a fall four days ago. Now drowsy, GCS 13; CT shows a left subdural haematoma with 9 mm midline shift.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has a fusiform, flexed index finger two days after a thorn prick, with flexor sheath tenderness and pain on passive extension.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man in ICU with septic acute kidney injury has serum potassium 7.6 mmol/L. ECG shows broad QRS complexes and absent P waves.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner 6 weeks after she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Before the diagnosis she had 10 weeks of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal cramps. Stool pathogen tests were negative. Ileocolonoscopy found continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 30 cm and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. Biopsies showed crypt distortion with no granulomas and no dysplasia. She now takes oral mesalazine and mesalazine enemas. She has 1 to 2 formed stools a day with no blood. She has never smoked. Her mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 62. No other relatives have had bowel cancer. Temperature is 36.7°C, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and pulse 72/min. Her abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 129 g/L (115–165), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), ALP 74 U/L (30–110) and GGT 18 U/L (<40). She asks how her bowel cancer risk will be checked.

CT colonography every 5 years starting now

After that, the interval (1, 3 or 5 years) is set by risk factors such as ongoing inflammation, strictures, past dysplasia, PSC and family history. Her mother's cancer at 62 may shorten later intervals, but it does not change the start point. Population or family-history screening does not apply to her, because her colitis is the bigger risk and needs colonoscopy with targeted biopsies. Annual colonoscopy straight away is only for coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.

CT colonography cannot take biopsies or show flat dysplasia, so it is not used for surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease.

items.stem: A 52-year-old Aboriginal man from Arnhem Land with type 2 diabetes presents in February with fever, productive cough and right upper lobe consolidation. Temperature 39.4 °C.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to her back. BP is 84/50 mmHg. CT aortogram shows an ascending aortic intimal flap with haemopericardium.

items.stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a headache that has got steadily worse over 6 hours. The headache is generalised and throbbing, and he has fever, rigors, vomiting and pain when looking at lights. He has no history of headaches, head injury or seizures, and he takes no medicines. His temperature is 39.3 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Neck flexion is painful and restricted. Fundoscopy shows sharp optic disc margins. Cranial nerve and limb examinations are normal, and there is no rash. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV. Laboratory studies show:
White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)
Platelets 245 x10^9/L (150 to 400)
INR 1.0 (0.9 to 1.2)
C-reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5)
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This man has fever, a headache that built up over hours, photophobia and neck stiffness, so he has bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. The right first steps have been taken: blood cultures, then dexamethasone and ceftriaxone without waiting for any test. Lumbar puncture is the next investigation. CSF cell count, protein, glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture with susceptibilities and PCR confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism and guide how antibiotics are narrowed and how long they are given. Under eTG, CT before LP is needed only if there is a contraindication: reduced or falling GCS, focal neurological signs, a recent seizure, papilloedema or immunocompromise. He has none of these. His platelets and INR are normal, so it is safe to go straight to LP. Organisms can often still be found in CSF in the first hours after antibiotics, and cell count, protein and glucose changes last longer, so LP should be done promptly and not put off.
why: Correct: with GCS 15, no focal signs, no seizure, no papilloedema and normal platelets and coagulation, LP is safe without imaging, and CSF analysis is the test that confirms bacterial meningitis and identifies the organism.
MRI with contrast can show meningeal enhancement or complications, but it is slow, hard to get in the ED and does not identify the organism or confirm bacterial meningitis.
CT angiography looks for an aneurysm in subarachnoid haemorrhage, which is unlikely here because the headache built up over 6 hours with high fever and was not a thunderclap onset.
Blood meningococcal PCR is a useful extra test, especially after antibiotics, but it detects only one organism and does not replace CSF analysis as the test that confirms meningitis.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man from the Philippines has 8 weeks of productive cough, night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows left upper lobe cavitation.
items.ask: Test most likely to confirm diagnosis?
items.explanation: A chronic productive cough with night sweats, weight loss, birth in a high-TB country and upper lobe cavitation points to active pulmonary TB. The diagnosis is confirmed by three sputum samples sent for AFB microscopy, mycobacterial culture and NAAT. NAAT gives a fast result and detects rifampicin resistance, and culture provides full drug susceptibility testing.
why: An IGRA detects immune sensitisation to TB, not active disease, so it cannot confirm active TB and may be negative in active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease and is less specific after BCG vaccination, which is common in people born in the Philippines.
CT shows the extent of disease in more detail but cannot identify the organism, so it does not confirm TB.
Bronchoscopy is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum is negative, and this man has a productive cough.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-204

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 days of cough productive of green sputum, fevers, and left-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration. Six days ago she was discharged from hospital after a 4-day admission to investigate syncope. On the ward she walked daily and received prophylactic enoxaparin. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and has never smoked. She has no haemoptysis and no history of venous thromboembolism or cancer. Her temperature is 38.5 °C, pulse 106/min, respirations 24/min, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, and SpO2 93% on room air. There is dullness and bronchial breathing at the left base. Both calves are soft and nontender, and there is no leg swelling. A chest X-ray shows new consolidation in the left lower lobe. Results: white cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), CRP 151 mg/L (less than 5), urea 7.9 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.5), D-dimer 0.63 mg/L FEU (less than 0.50).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating her for pulmonary embolism?
items.explanation: Start by working out her pre-test probability. Her Wells score is 1.5: she gets 1.5 for a heart rate over 100/min and nothing else. She was not immobilised, because she walked daily on the ward and had prophylactic enoxaparin. She had no surgery, her calves are normal, she has no haemoptysis, no past VTE and no cancer, and pneumonia explains her illness better than PE does. A Wells score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely, so a D-dimer is the right test to rule it out. In patients over 50, the D-dimer cut-off is age-adjusted: age x 0.01 mg/L FEU, which is 0.71 mg/L for a 71-year-old. Her D-dimer of 0.63 mg/L is above the standard laboratory limit of 0.50 but below her age-adjusted cut-off. This is a negative result, and with low pre-test probability it excludes PE (eTG Cardiovascular; ADJUST-PE). She needs no further tests for PE. The next step is to manage the left lower lobe pneumonia, which began soon after a hospital stay. CT pulmonary angiography is wrong because it is only needed if PE is likely (Wells over 4) or the D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cut-off. A V/Q scan is wrong because it is another imaging test for PE, used instead of CTPA when contrast is unsafe, and it is not needed once PE has been excluded. Compression ultrasound of the legs is wrong because her legs are normal on examination and PE has already been excluded. Repeating the D-dimer is wrong because the first result is already negative using the correct cut-off, and repeating it only delays treatment.
why: CT pulmonary angiography is wrong because it is only needed when PE is likely (Wells over 4) or the D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cut-off of 0.71 mg/L, and neither applies to her.

A V/Q scan is wrong because it is an alternative to CTPA for patients who cannot have contrast, and with a low Wells score and a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off she does not need imaging for PE.
Compression ultrasound of both legs is wrong because her calves are normal with no swelling, and a negative D-dimer with low pre-test probability has already excluded thromboembolism.
Repeating the D-dimer is wrong because the first result is already negative using the correct cut-off, so a repeat adds nothing and delays treatment of her pneumonia.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has a 3-month non-healing ulcer with raised, everted edges. It arose within a scar from a childhood flame burn to his thigh. The scar had been stable for 50 years.
items.explanation: A Marjolin ulcer is a cancer that grows in a chronic wound or an old burn scar, usually decades after the injury, and it is most often squamous cell carcinoma. Any non-healing ulcer in an old scar needs a biopsy to rule out SCC. These tumours spread to lymph nodes more aggressively than ordinary cutaneous SCC.
why: BCC can occasionally arise in a burn scar, but it is much less common than SCC there and usually looks pearly with a rolled edge rather than everted.
Melanoma rarely arises in burn scars, and this lesion shows no pigment or change in a pre-existing mole.
Merkel cell carcinoma is a fast-growing red nodule on sun-damaged skin, not a slowly developing ulcer in a chronic scar.
DFSP is a slow-growing firm plaque on the trunk of young adults and is not linked to chronic burn scars.

source.name: Written by AI for Plastic Surgery (no Med-OS station)

items.stem: A 42-year-old Aboriginal man with type 2 diabetes attends his annual health check. eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73 m². His urine albumin:creatinine ratio is 14 mg/mmol on two separate samples taken over three months.
items.explanation: A urine ACR that stays between 2.5 and 25 mg/mmol in a man (Kidney Health Australia; KDIGO A2 is 3 to 30) is moderately increased albuminuria, also called microalbuminuria. With an eGFR of 82, this means stage 2 chronic kidney disease, most likely early diabetic kidney disease. This group is at high risk, so he needs an ACE inhibitor or ARB and tight control of blood pressure, glucose and cardiovascular risk.
why: Wrong: severely increased albuminuria in a man is an ACR above 25 mg/mmol (KDIGO above 30), and 14 is below that.
Wrong: normal albumin excretion in a man is an ACR below 2.5 mg/mmol, so 14 mg/mmol is clearly abnormal.
Wrong: nephrotic-range loss means an ACR of roughly 220 mg/mmol or more, far above 14 mg/mmol.
Wrong: a transient rise after exercise would not stay high on two separate samples taken months apart.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 hours after he was punched in the face outside a hotel. He says both sides of his nose are blocked and his nose is painful. He had a nosebleed that stopped on its own after 10 minutes. He has no clear fluid running from his nose, no double vision and no headache. He takes no regular medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The nasal bridge is swollen and bent to the left. After phenylephrine–lidocaine spray, anterior rhinoscopy shows a smooth, red-purple swelling on both sides of the septum that blocks both nostrils. The swelling has not shrunk and feels soft and fluctuant when pressed with a cotton bud. Eye movements are full, cheek sensation is normal and his bite is normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day incision and drainage with bilateral nasal packing
Closed reduction of the nasal bones in 7 days
Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate with review in 48 hours
Silver nitrate cautery to the anterior septum
CT of the facial bones before specialist review
items.explanation: This man has a bilateral nasal septal haematoma. After a blow to the nose he has blockage on both sides, and on both sides of the septum there is a smooth, red-purple, fluctuant swelling that does not shrink with a decongestant. Septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and gets its nutrients from the overlying mucoperichondrium. Blood collecting under the perichondrium lifts it off the cartilage. Within about 24 to 72 hours this can cause cartilage necrosis and infection. The results are a septal abscess, which can spread to the cavernous sinus or the meninges, a septal perforation and a saddle nose deformity. Bilateral haematomas carry the highest risk. The aim is to prevent these complications, so the haematoma must be drained the same day, by ENT or by a trained emergency doctor: incise and drain each side, then use bilateral packing or septal splints to stop it filling again. He should also have antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus (as advised in Therapeutic Guidelines) and early ENT follow-up. The displaced nasal fractures can be reduced later, once the swelling settles. Safety-net advice: return straight away if the blockage comes back, or if he develops fever, more pain or a change in the shape of his nose.
why: Delayed closed reduction is right for the displaced nasal bone fracture on its own, but a 7-day wait would let the septal cartilage die and become infected.
Antibiotics are added after drainage, but on their own they cannot remove the blood starving the cartilage, so the necrosis and abscess risk stays.
Cautery treats bleeding from vessels in Little's area; it does nothing for a blood collection under the perichondrium, and his nosebleed has already stopped.
This is a clinical diagnosis, he has no features of a naso-orbito-ethmoid, orbital or other facial fracture, and waiting for imaging delays drainage that should not be delayed.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to a general practice in July because of a dry cough that started suddenly 3 days ago. She also has fevers, muscle aches, fatigue, a sore throat and a blocked nose. Two colleagues at the café where she works have had similar symptoms this week. She has no breathlessness or chest pain. She has no history of serious illness, takes no medicines, is not pregnant and did not have an influenza vaccine this year. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily. Her temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 96/min, respiratory rate 16/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert and talking in full sentences. The pharynx is mildly red without exudate. The chest is clear to auscultation. A multiplex nasopharyngeal PCR swab shows: influenza A RNA detected; influenza B RNA not detected; SARS-CoV-2 RNA not detected; respiratory syncytial virus RNA not detected; Bordetella pertussis DNA not detected.
items.ask: Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days
Paracetamol, fluids and rest, avoiding contact with others until well
Chest X-ray within the next 24 hours
Repeat SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test in 48 hours
items.explanation: The PCR confirms influenza A and rules out SARS-CoV-2, RSV and pertussis. Her observations show fever and a high-normal heart rate, but her respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and blood pressure are normal, she is alert and her chest is clear. Together these results mean uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult. She has no complications and no risk factors for severe disease (she is not pregnant, not immunocompromised and has no chronic heart or lung disease). The right management is symptom relief with paracetamol, fluids and rest. She should stay away from work and other people until she is well, and use cough etiquette and hand hygiene. She should also be offered next season's influenza vaccine and brief smoking cessation advice, and told to seek urgent care if she becomes breathless at rest, gets chest pain or confusion, or gets worse again after improving. eTG keeps oseltamivir for severe illness or people at higher risk. In healthy adults it only modestly shortens symptoms, and only when started within 48 hours of onset. She is at day 3. Antibiotics do not help a viral infection when there is no sign of bacterial pneumonia. A chest X-ray is not needed when the chest is clear and saturation is normal. A negative multiplex PCR is more sensitive than a rapid antigen test, and another cause has already been found.
why: Wrong: oseltamivir is for severe illness or higher-risk patients, and she is a healthy, non-pregnant adult at day 3, past the 48-hour window where it helps a little.
Wrong: the illness is confirmed viral, with a clear chest and normal saturation, so there is no sign of bacterial pneumonia that would justify antibiotics.
Wrong: a clear chest, normal respiratory rate and 98% saturation on room air give no sign of pneumonia, so imaging would not change management.
Wrong: a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR is more sensitive than a rapid antigen test, and influenza A already explains her illness, so retesting adds nothing.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is in the terminal phase, unresponsive, with noisy gurgling breathing. He appears comfortable; repositioning has not helped and his family is distressed.
items.explanation: This is noisy breathing from respiratory secretions in a dying patient. Repositioning has not helped, so eTG Palliative Care recommends a subcutaneous anticholinergic such as hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg. Explaining to the family that the noise is not distressing him is also part of care. Anticholinergics reduce new secretions but do not clear secretions that are already there, so start early.
why: The secretions sit in the pharynx and airway, not as pulmonary oedema, so a diuretic will not help and IV access burdens a dying patient.
Midazolam treats terminal agitation or distress, and he looks comfortable, so it does nothing for the secretions.
Morphine relieves breathlessness or pain, neither of which he has, and it does not reduce secretions.
Deep suction is distressing, can stimulate more secretions and is not recommended; only gentle oral suction is sometimes used.

source.name: Written by AI for Palliative Care (no Med-OS station)

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 8 hours of constant, severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back, with repeated vomiting. The pain began 2 hours after a large evening meal. She drinks 2 standard drinks on weekends and does not smoke. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rigidity and no jaundice. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Results: lipase 2400 U/L (reference <60), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 40 mg/L, total bilirubin 22 µmol/L (<20), ALT 186 U/L (<35), ALP 140 U/L (30–110), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L and creatinine 78 µmol/L. IV fluids and titrated opioid analgesia have been started.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pancreas
items.explanation: She already meets 2 of the 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis: typical epigastric pain going through to the back, and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit. The diagnosis is made, so the next step is to find the cause. Gallstones cause about half of all cases. An early ALT above about 150 U/L strongly suggests a biliary cause, and her obesity and diabetes add to the risk. Her calcium and triglycerides are normal and she drinks little alcohol. Australian guidance (eTG) and international guidance say every patient with acute pancreatitis should have a transabdominal ultrasound on admission to look for gallstones and a dilated bile duct. This is because a gallstone cause changes management: ERCP if there is cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, and cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. The test is quick, cheap, uses no radiation and can be done at the bedside. Early contrast CT does not help when the diagnosis is already clear. ERCP is for cholangitis or a proven obstruction that persists. MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are second-line tests for when the ultrasound is unclear or no cause is found. Amylase adds nothing once the lipase is raised.
why: Contrast CT is for when the diagnosis is uncertain, or for looking for necrosis if she deteriorates after 72 hours; the diagnosis is already made, and CT in the first days underestimates necrosis and is poor at showing gallstones.
ERCP is invasive, carries a risk of making pancreatitis worse, and in the early phase is only for cholangitis or a proven persisting bile duct obstruction, neither of which has been shown here.
MRCP is a second-line test for suspected duct stones when the ultrasound is unclear or the liver tests stay abnormal; it should not come before the first-line ultrasound.
Amylase is less specific than lipase and clears sooner, so it adds nothing to a lipase already more than 30 times the upper limit and does not show the cause.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-214

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has had painful swelling of both wrists and MCP joints for 3 months, with 90 minutes of morning stiffness. His DIP joints are spared, and his skin and nails are normal.
items.ask: Which blood test best confirms the diagnosis?
items.explanation: He has symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of the wrists and MCPs with long morning stiffness and spared DIPs, which points to rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP antibodies are about 95% specific for RA, so they are the best test to confirm it. A strongly positive result also predicts erosive disease.
why: Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but not specific, because it is also positive in infection, Sjögren's, older people and other connective tissue diseases.
ANA is used to screen for SLE, and his history has no lupus features; ANA is also often positive in RA, so it cannot confirm it.
HLA-B27 is linked with spondyloarthritis, which usually causes axial or asymmetrical large-joint disease rather than symmetrical small-joint synovitis.
Serum urate does not confirm gout, which usually causes acute attacks in single joints, and urate is often normal during an attack.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-194

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has four months of bloating, pale loose stools and fatigue. Ferritin is 8 microgram/L; tTG-IgA is 96 U/mL with normal total IgA.
items.explanation: He has malabsorption, iron deficiency and a strongly positive tTG-IgA with normal total IgA. In Australian adults, coeliac disease must be confirmed with duodenal biopsies at gastroscopy while the patient is still eating gluten. The gluten-free diet starts only after the diagnosis is confirmed.
why: Starting a gluten-free diet before biopsy can heal the villi and make the histology falsely normal, so the diagnosis can no longer be confirmed.
Waiting to repeat strongly positive serology delays the diagnosis and adds nothing, because the result is already reliable with a normal total IgA.
HLA typing is mainly useful for ruling coeliac disease out because of its high negative predictive value; a positive result cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Colonoscopy looks at the colon and terminal ileum, not the proximal small bowel where coeliac disease causes damage, so it is not the next step here.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-303

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with newly confirmed HIV-1 infection has a CD4 count of 480 cells/µL and osteoporosis on DXA. His doctor plans dolutegravir, abacavir and lamivudine rather than tenofovir.
items.explanation: ASHM guidelines say to screen for HLA-B*5701 before starting abacavir. Carriers have a high risk of a hypersensitivity reaction that can be fatal, so a positive result rules the drug out. A negative result makes abacavir a safe choice for a patient who needs to avoid tenofovir because of bone disease.
why: HLA-B*1502 predicts Stevens-Johnson syndrome with carbamazepine in people of Asian ancestry, not abacavir hypersensitivity.
TPMT activity guides the dose of azathioprine or mercaptopurine and has no role before antiretroviral therapy.
G6PD deficiency matters for drugs such as dapsone or primaquine, not for this regimen.
A co-receptor tropism assay is needed only before maraviroc, which is not part of this regimen.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station ai-8bb4689d

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has a 9 mm pigmented lesion on his back that has grown over three months. Dermoscopy shows irregular borders and variegated colour.
items.explanation: A changing pigmented lesion with irregular borders and variegated colour is suspicious for melanoma. Australian melanoma guidelines recommend complete excisional biopsy with 2 mm margins, which confirms the diagnosis and gives an accurate Breslow thickness. The definitive margins and the need for sentinel node biopsy are then decided from that thickness.
why: A shave biopsy can cut through the base of the lesion, so the Breslow thickness cannot be measured and staging is wrong.
A punch biopsy samples only part of a lesion this size, so it can miss the deepest or most atypical area and under-stage or miss the melanoma.
Wide local excision before a tissue diagnosis has no Breslow thickness to set the margins and can disrupt lymphatic drainage needed for sentinel node mapping.
Short-term digital monitoring is for flat lesions with low suspicion, not a lesion already growing with features of melanoma.

source.name: Written by AI for Plastic Surgery (no Med-OS station)

items.stem: A 62-year-old female smoker with type 2 diabetes presents to vascular clinic with 3 weeks of forefoot rest pain eased by dependency. No pedal pulses, dry gangrene of three toes, ABI 0.28.
items.ask: Most likely cause of death within 5 years?
items.explanation: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia is a marker of widespread atherosclerosis. Up to half of patients die within 5 years, mostly from coronary and cerebrovascular events. That is why an antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP and glucose control and stopping smoking are part of her treatment, alongside revascularisation.
why: Dry gangrene can become wet and cause sepsis, but this is a threat to the limb and a less common cause of death than coronary events.
She is less mobile, but PE causes far fewer deaths in PAD than heart attack or stroke.
Smoking raises her risk of lung cancer, but over 5 years her risk of dying from heart disease is much higher.
Aortic aneurysm is linked to PAD, but rupture causes only a small share of deaths, and fewer in women.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-625

items.stem: A 48-year-old man reports three spontaneous hours-long attacks of spinning vertigo with left tinnitus. Left audiometry: air and bone thresholds 45 dB at 250–500 Hz, normal from 2000 Hz. Right ear normal.
items.explanation: Air and bone thresholds are equal, so there is no air-bone gap and the loss is sensorineural. It affects only 250–500 Hz and recovers by 2000 Hz, so it is a low-frequency loss. A documented one-sided low-frequency sensorineural loss with spontaneous attacks of vertigo lasting hours meets the Bárány criteria for Ménière's disease, and because the loss is asymmetric he also needs ENT referral.
why: A conductive loss needs bone conduction better than air conduction (an air-bone gap), and here the two thresholds are equal.
The thresholds are normal from 2000 Hz upward, so the high frequencies are spared; a high-frequency loss suggests presbycusis or a vestibular schwannoma.
A mixed loss needs both raised bone thresholds and an air-bone gap, and there is no gap here.
Noise-induced loss causes a dip around 4000 Hz, but here the loss is at 250–500 Hz and the high frequencies are normal.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-190

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman, a former smoker, has 3 months of breathlessness and 9 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a large left pleural effusion. SpO2 94% on room air.
items.explanation: A new, large, one-sided effusion with weight loss in a former smoker needs a diagnosis. Ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration both diagnoses and relieves it. Send fluid for protein, LDH, pH, glucose, cell count, cytology and culture, remove no more than about 1.5 L at once, and get a contrast CT chest ideally before full drainage.
why: Frusemide treats heart failure, but a large effusion on one side with weight loss and no features of heart failure needs fluid analysis, not a trial of diuretics.
A chest drain is not the first step for an undiagnosed effusion in a stable patient: it is more invasive and is kept for empyema, pneumothorax or planned pleurodesis.
Pleurodesis is only done once a recurrent malignant effusion is confirmed and the lung has been shown to re-expand.
Bronchoscopy comes later, guided by CT, and has a low yield before then, while sampling the pleural fluid is less invasive and may make the diagnosis.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-582

items.stem: A 33-year-old man who works as a mechanic sees his general practitioner because of tiredness for 4 months. He drinks about 4 L of water a day. He gets up three times a night to pass urine, even when he avoids drinks in the evening. He has gained 15 kg over 2 years and has not lost weight recently. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His father has type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His BMI is 36 kg/m². He has velvety, darkened skin in both axillae and looks well hydrated. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, protein negative and specific gravity 1.025. A random fingerprick reading on the practice meter is 15.2 mmol/L.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This man has the typical symptoms of hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria and nocturia that continues when he drinks less in the evening. He also has metabolic risk factors: obesity, acanthosis nigricans, hypertension, smoking and a family history of type 2 diabetes. His urine is concentrated and full of glucose, and he has no ketones, which points to type 2 diabetes. A fingerprick meter reading is not enough to diagnose diabetes, so the RACGP handbook and eTG require a laboratory test. HbA1c is the most appropriate test. A level of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more diagnoses diabetes, he does not need to fast for it, and Medicare funds it for diagnosis. Because he has symptoms, one abnormal laboratory result is enough and no repeat test on another day is needed. A fasting or random venous plasma glucose would also be acceptable, but neither is among the options. An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal results or pregnancy. The water deprivation test, GAD antibodies and C-peptide do not confirm that he has diabetes.
why: An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal fasting (5.5 to 6.9 mmol/L) or random (5.5 to 11.0 mmol/L) glucose results or for pregnancy, and it is unnecessary and burdensome in a patient with symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia.

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, but his urine is concentrated (specific gravity 1.025) and full of glucose, which shows an osmotic diuresis, and fluid restriction could make his dehydration worse.

GAD antibodies help classify suspected type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (for example in a lean patient with weight loss or ketosis), but they do not confirm that diabetes is present.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the pancreas can still make and helps classify the type of diabetes, but it does not diagnose diabetes and can be misleadingly low during hyperglycaemia.

source.name: Written by AI from Med-OS station amsa-381

items.stem: A 29-year-old man who has sex with men has a 10-day painless, indurated penile ulcer. Syphilis EIA and TPPA are positive; RPR is 1:32. No drug allergies.
items.explanation: A painless indurated chancre with positive treponemal tests and a reactive RPR means primary syphilis. Under the Australian STI Management Guidelines and eTG, the treatment is a single dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units IM. Syphilis must also be notified, sexual contacts traced, and HIV and other STIs tested for.
why: A single dose of ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea but is not enough to treat syphilis.
Azithromycin is not recommended for syphilis because macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread.
Doxycycline is only the alternative for penicillin allergy, and it needs 14 days for early syphilis, not 7.
Valaciclovir treats genital herpes, which causes painful multiple ulcers and negative treponemal serology.

source.name: Written by AI for Sexual Health (no Med-OS station)

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to a general practice because of recurrent headaches over the past 3 months. She has had four attacks. Each begins with shimmering zigzag lights in one half of her vision that spread slowly over 20 minutes and then clear completely. Within 30 minutes, a throbbing one-sided headache follows, with nausea and sensitivity to light and noise, and lasts about 18 hours. The side varies between attacks, and she is well in between. Her mother has a similar history. She uses a copper intrauterine device, takes ibuprofen during attacks and takes no regular medicines. She is worried that she has a brain tumour. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 76/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. There is no neck stiffness. A full neurological examination is normal, including fundoscopy, which shows sharp discs and spontaneous venous pulsations.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: MRI of the brain with gadolinium
items.explanation: This woman has recurrent, stereotyped attacks that meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura. The aura is a positive visual disturbance that spreads gradually over more than 5 minutes, lasts under 60 minutes, resolves fully and is followed within an hour by a throbbing, unilateral headache with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia. The side varies, she is well between attacks, she has a family history, and her neurological examination and fundi are normal. Migraine is a clinical diagnosis. eTG (Neurology) states that a typical history with a normal examination and no red flags needs no neuroimaging. The most useful next investigation is a diary she keeps from now on, recording when each attack happens, the aura, how long it lasts, triggers, acute medicine days and menstrual timing. The diary confirms the stereotyped pattern and flags any change that would point to a secondary cause. It also counts medicine days to detect medication overuse and gives the attack frequency needed to decide on preventive treatment. Reassure her and explain why she does not need a scan, rather than ordering imaging to ease her worry.
why: MRI is kept for red flags such as an atypical or prolonged aura, a changed pattern, abnormal examination findings or papilloedema, none of which she has, so a scan would not change management.

Non-contrast CT is used for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage or acute intracranial pathology, but her headaches build up gradually after an aura in a recurrent pattern, and she would receive radiation for no diagnostic benefit.

CT venography is used when cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, for example with a persistent progressive headache, papilloedema or a prothrombotic risk such as oestrogen use, but she has discrete attacks, normal fundi and a non-hormonal contraceptive.

Electroencephalography is used to investigate seizures, and occipital seizures cause brief coloured circular images lasting seconds to a few minutes, not the slowly spreading zigzag aura followed by migraine headache that she describes.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man who drinks heavily presents with two weeks of increasing abdominal distension. Serum albumin is 28 g/L. Ascitic fluid albumin is 7 g/L and total protein 8 g/L.
items.ask: What does this ascitic result indicate?
items.explanation: The serum-ascites albumin gradient is 28 − 7 = 21 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertensive ascites, which in a heavy drinker is most likely from alcohol-related cirrhosis. Ascitic protein below 10 g/L also puts him at high risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
why: Peritoneal malignancy gives a SAAG below 11 g/L, usually with high ascitic protein.
Tuberculous peritonitis gives a low SAAG with high protein and a lymphocyte-rich fluid.
Nephrotic syndrome gives a SAAG below 11 g/L, because the ascites comes from hypoalbuminaemia, not portal hypertension.
Pancreatic ascites gives a low SAAG with a very high ascitic amylase.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man who smokes has 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Erect chest X-ray shows a dense right opacity with a concave meniscus reaching the 2nd rib. The trachea is deviated left.
items.explanation: A dense opacity with a concave meniscus that pushes the trachea and mediastinum to the other side is a large pleural effusion: the fluid takes up space. Anything that causes volume loss on the right, such as collapse or pneumonectomy, would pull the trachea towards the opacity instead. In a heavy smoker, this calls for ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration and a CT to look for malignancy.
why: Collapse causes volume loss, so the trachea would be pulled towards the right, not pushed away to the left.
Consolidation does not change lung volume, so the trachea would stay central. It usually shows air bronchograms rather than a meniscus.
After a pneumonectomy the mediastinum moves towards the empty hemithorax, so the trachea would shift right.
A raised hemidiaphragm keeps its domed outline, has no meniscus, does not reach the 2nd rib and does not push the trachea away.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner for her annual diabetes review. She has had type 2 diabetes for 14 years. Over the past 4 months, small print has become harder to read with her right eye, even with new reading glasses. She also has hypertension and dyslipidaemia. Her medicines are metformin 1 g twice daily, modified-release gliclazide 60 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Her last eye examination was 2 years ago. Blood pressure is 144/86 mmHg and pulse is 76/min. Visual acuity is 6/18 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left, and the right eye does not improve with a pinhole. Both lenses are clear. Good-quality non-mydriatic retinal photographs show microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages in both eyes, and a ring of hard exudates within one disc diameter of the right fovea. There are no new vessels and no venous beading. HbA1c is 8.8% (73 mmol/mol).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of the reduced vision in her right eye?
items.explanation: She has non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. In the right eye she has hard exudates near the fovea and slowly worsening central vision that a pinhole does not correct, so a refractive error is not the cause. This pattern points to diabetic macular oedema, which causes most vision loss in diabetes and can occur at any stage of retinopathy. Retinal photographs are two-dimensional and cannot show retinal thickening, so they cannot confirm or exclude macular oedema. The NHMRC diabetic retinopathy guideline and the RACGP handbook advise referral to an ophthalmologist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the non-invasive test that confirms the diagnosis. It measures central retinal thickness, shows intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and is used to decide on and monitor anti-VEGF treatment. Fluorescein angiography is an invasive second-line test. Ultrasound is only needed when the fundus cannot be seen. Visual field testing and repeat photographs cannot assess retinal thickness.
why: Fluorescein angiography is invasive, carries a risk of dye reactions, and is kept for assessing ischaemia or new vessels or for planning laser, so it is not the first test to confirm macular oedema.
B-scan ultrasound is used when the view of the retina is blocked, for example by vitreous haemorrhage or dense cataract, but her lenses are clear and the fundus can be seen.
Automated perimetry tests peripheral visual fields for glaucoma or neurological disease, and it cannot show the structural macular changes behind her central blur.
Repeat photographs after dilation give a better view but are still two-dimensional, so they cannot measure retinal thickness or reliably exclude macular oedema.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman, para 3, is in the birth suite 40 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth of twins at 37 weeks' gestation. The placenta is complete and there are no genital tract tears. She keeps bleeding despite intramuscular oxytocin, an oxytocin infusion, intramuscular ergometrine, intramuscular carboprost, an indwelling urinary catheter and bimanual compression. She has been given intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g. The weighed blood loss is 2,000 mL and the blood contains clots. She has no history of a bleeding disorder and takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.3 °C, pulse is 130/min, blood pressure is 86/48 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min and SpO2 is 96% on 6 L/min of oxygen. The fundus is intermittently soft. Two 16-gauge cannulas are in place, the massive transfusion protocol has been activated, O-negative red cells are running and theatre is being prepared. Point-of-care haemoglobin is 82 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L).
items.ask: Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to guide further blood component replacement?
items.explanation: This woman has a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (2,000 mL and still bleeding) from uterine atony. Her risk factors are twins, which overdistend the uterus, and multiparity. Large blood loss leads to dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy, which makes the bleeding worse. In obstetric haemorrhage, fibrinogen is the first clotting factor to fall to a critical level. It falls well before the platelet count or the clotting times change. A fibrinogen level below 2 g/L is the best early lab predictor of progression to severe PPH. RANZCOG, the Queensland Clinical Guidelines and the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Module 5 all advise measuring it (Clauss fibrinogen, or FIBTEM on viscoelastic testing where available) and repeating it often. Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is given to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L. The fact that she is forming clots does not rule out a falling fibrinogen. D-dimer is normally raised in pregnancy and after birth, so it does not help guide replacement. APTT and PT stay normal until late in obstetric haemorrhage, so they are poor early guides. Platelets fall late, usually only after very large losses, so the count is not the best early guide. Haemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss, and red cells are already being given on clinical grounds, so a repeat level does not guide clotting factor replacement.
why: D-dimer is normally raised in pregnancy and the puerperium, so it cannot reliably detect coagulopathy or guide what to give.
The APTT stays normal until late in obstetric haemorrhage, so it misses the early fall in fibrinogen that drives ongoing bleeding.
The platelet count usually falls only after very large losses or with abruption or HELLP, so it is a late and poor guide here.
Haemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss and only measures red cells, so it cannot guide replacement of clotting factors.

items.stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by her father at 03:00 with noisy, fast breathing that started during the evening. She has had a runny nose and cough for 3 days, and several children at her child care centre have colds. Six months ago she had a similar episode during a cold, and it settled within 2 days. She has no cough or wheeze between colds, no choking episode, no new foods and no rash. She has eczema and her immunisations are up to date. Her father smokes outdoors. Her weight is 13 kg. Temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 42/min, blood pressure 96/60 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on room air. She is alert and talking in short phrases. She has mild subcostal recession and widespread expiratory wheeze, with equal air entry on both sides and no crackles. Inhaled salbutamol is about to be given.
items.ask: In addition to treatment, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
options: Repeated bedside review of response to bronchodilator
Full blood count and C-reactive protein
items.explanation: This toddler has a moderate episode of viral-induced (preschool) wheeze. She has a 3-day coryzal illness, then acute bilateral expiratory wheeze with recession, a similar episode with a previous cold, no symptoms between colds, and risk factors including eczema, child care and smoke exposure. There are no features of anaphylaxis or an inhaled foreign body. The diagnosis is clinical. The RCH acute asthma guideline and the Queensland preschool wheeze guideline grade severity, and confirm the diagnosis, by repeated bedside assessment. This covers mental state, work of breathing, ability to talk, air entry, respiratory rate and SpO2, checked after each salbutamol dose by spacer and mask and again at the end of the first hour. Improvement with a bronchodilator supports the diagnosis and guides the decision to admit or discharge. Routine chest X-ray, blood tests and blood gases are not recommended because they do not change management. Antibiotics are not indicated.
why: Correct: viral-induced wheeze is diagnosed and graded clinically, and serial review of work of breathing, talking, air entry and SpO2 after salbutamol both confirms the diagnosis and directs further management.

A chest X-ray is not routine in preschool wheeze because it seldom changes management; with equal air entry, no crackles and no choking episode, there is no suspicion of pneumonia, pneumothorax or a foreign body.
A blood gas is reserved for severe or life-threatening episodes not responding to treatment, and it is not needed in an alert child with moderate distress and SpO2 of 94%.
Children under about 6 years cannot reliably perform spirometry, and it has no place in assessing an acute episode.

items.stem:
A 25-year-old man attends a hospital pre-admission clinic before a planned colonoscopy. He has had 2 years of intermittent loose stools, crampy right iliac fossa pain, recurrent mouth ulcers and an unintentional 6 kg weight loss. He sometimes wakes at night to open his bowels. His GP started ferrous sulfate tablets 3 weeks ago. He eats a normal diet that includes bread and pasta and takes no other medicines. His temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His conjunctivae are pale, and he has mild right iliac fossa tenderness with no palpable mass. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 118 g/L (135–175)
MCV 76 fL (80–100)
Platelets 448 x10^9/L (150–400)
Ferritin 16 µg/L (30–500)
Transferrin saturation 8% (20–50)
CRP 28 mg/L (less than 5)
Albumin 31 g/L (35–50)
Vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (150–700)
Faecal calprotectin 520 µg/g (less than 50)
items.ask: Which of the following best explains this patient's blood count findings?
options: Anaemia of inflammation with replete iron stores
Vitamin B12 deficiency from terminal ileal disease
Absolute iron deficiency with coexisting inflammation
Folate deficiency from small bowel malabsorption
items.explanation: This man probably has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. His raised CRP, platelets and calprotectin and his low albumin show active inflammation, and he has a microcytic anaemia (Hb 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL). Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation pushes it up. A ferritin of 16 µg/L despite a CRP of 28 mg/L, and despite 3 weeks of oral iron, therefore confirms that his iron stores are truly empty. In active IBD, a ferritin below 100 µg/L already suggests iron deficiency, and below 30 µg/L confirms it. A transferrin saturation of 8% supports this. The likely causes are blood loss from ulcerated mucosa and poor absorption. What this means for him: he needs his iron replaced, and IV iron (for example ferric carboxymaltose) is preferred because oral iron is poorly absorbed and poorly tolerated in active IBD. He should also stop the oral iron 5 to 7 days before colonoscopy. Anaemia of inflammation alone would give a normal or high ferritin. B12 deficiency and folate deficiency both cause a large-cell (macrocytic) anaemia, and his B12 is normal. Thalassaemia trait does not cause a low ferritin or a low transferrin saturation.
why: Wrong: anaemia of inflammation alone gives a normal or raised ferritin, but his ferritin of 16 µg/L is low even though inflammation should be pushing it up.
Wrong: terminal ileal disease can cause B12 deficiency, but that gives a macrocytic anaemia, and his B12 of 380 pmol/L is normal.
Wrong: thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal or high iron stores, so it would not explain a ferritin of 16 µg/L and a transferrin saturation of 8%.
Wrong: folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, not a microcytic one with an MCV of 76 fL and low iron studies.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with newly confirmed HIV-1 infection feels well and asks if he has AIDS. CD4 count is 450 cells/µL (24%), CD4:CD8 ratio 0.5, viral load 60,000 copies/mL.
items.ask: Best interpretation of the CD4 result?
items.explanation: A CD4 count of 450 cells/µL (24%) is below the normal range. The inverted CD4:CD8 ratio is typical of HIV. The count is still well above the AIDS thresholds of 200 cells/µL and 14%, so his immunity is mostly intact and he does not need Pneumocystis prophylaxis. Viral load, not CD4, is the main marker of how well ART works, and ART is recommended whatever the CD4 count.
why: CD4 450 cells/µL (24%) is mildly reduced but well above 200 cells/µL and 14%, so his immune system is mostly intact and this is not AIDS.
His CD4 count is below the usual reference range and his CD4:CD8 ratio is inverted, so his immune function is not normal.
Immune reconstitution is a rise in CD4 count on ART, and he has not started treatment.
A low CD4 count with an inverted ratio is what you expect in confirmed HIV, so there is no reason to think the result is a laboratory error.
