items.stem: A 68-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of difficulty swallowing for 10 weeks. Bread and meat feel as if they stick behind his lower sternum a few seconds after he swallows. He now cuts food into small pieces but drinks fluids easily. He has no choking, coughing, nasal regurgitation or hoarseness. He has lost 6 kg without trying and feels tired. He has had heartburn for about 20 years and treats it on and off using over-the-counter antacids. He smoked 30 pack-years until 5 years ago. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 136/82 mm Hg and BMI 34 kg/m². He has conjunctival pallor. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Haemoglobin is 116 g/L (reference 130–180), mean corpuscular volume 76 fL (80–100) and ferritin 10 µg/L (30–500).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: He has progressive dysphagia to solids only, with food sticking after the swallow. This suggests a mechanical oesophageal obstruction. He also has alarm features: weight loss, fatigue and iron deficiency anaemia. His risk factors for distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma are long-standing untreated reflux (a possible Barrett's oesophagus), obesity and a smoking history. The Australian optimal care pathway for oesophagogastric cancer recommends urgent gastroscopy, ideally within 2 weeks, for dysphagia with alarm features. Gastroscopy shows the mucosa directly and allows biopsies, which give the tissue diagnosis needed to confirm cancer, and it can also find Barrett's mucosa or a benign peptic stricture. A barium swallow cannot provide tissue and would delay the endoscopy he needs anyway. CT is used for staging once a cancer is proven by biopsy. Manometry is for suspected motility disorders, and only after endoscopy has ruled out an obstruction. Testing for Helicobacter pylori does not investigate dysphagia and is not appropriate when there are alarm features.
why: A barium swallow cannot take tissue for diagnosis, and any abnormality would still need endoscopy, so it delays the diagnosis.
CT is used to stage an oesophageal cancer after biopsy has confirmed it, and it cannot provide tissue for diagnosis.
Manometry assesses motility disorders such as achalasia, which cause dysphagia to solids and liquids, and should only be done after endoscopy rules out a mechanical cause.
A urea breath test looks for Helicobacter pylori in uncomplicated dyspepsia and does not investigate dysphagia with alarm features.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had confusion, polyuria and constipation for three days. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her corrected calcium is 3.6 mmol/L.
items.explanation: This is severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia of malignancy, and the patient is dehydrated from polyuria. The first step is IV rehydration with 0.9% sodium chloride, which restores volume and increases calcium excretion by the kidneys. An IV bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid is given once she is rehydrated (eTG).
why: Zoledronic acid is the right second step, but it takes 2 to 4 days to work and can harm the kidneys if given before rehydration.
Furosemide worsens dehydration and is now used only for fluid overload once the patient has been rehydrated.
Denosumab is kept for hypercalcaemia that does not respond to bisphosphonates or for severe renal impairment, not for first treatment.
Steroids help mainly in hypercalcaemia driven by calcitriol (lymphoma, granulomatous disease), not in bone metastases from breast cancer.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 8 days of fever, malaise and anorexia, followed by a right upper quadrant ache and dark urine. He returned 16 days ago from 6 weeks volunteering in a rural village in Papua New Guinea, where he drank untreated water and was often bitten by mosquitoes. He had no pre-travel vaccines, took no chemoprophylaxis and takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. He is alert and his sclerae are mildly icteric. The liver edge is tender 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen is not palpable. Results: ALT 2460 U/L (<35), ALP 155 U/L (30–110), bilirubin 46 µmol/L (<20), INR 1.1 and platelets 198 x10^9/L. Hepatitis A IgM is detected. A rapid Plasmodium antigen test is negative and one blood film shows no parasites. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled gallbladder with no stones and a common bile duct of normal calibre.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat malaria microscopy in 12 to 24 hours
items.explanation: This unvaccinated traveller has acute hepatitis A. He has a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury (ALT in the thousands with ALP only slightly raised), a positive hepatitis A IgM, and an incubation period that fits. His synthetic function is preserved (INR 1.1). However, he has a fever after travel to a highly malaria-endemic area with mosquito exposure and no prophylaxis, so malaria has to be actively excluded, even though another diagnosis has been found. Co-infection is possible, and missing falciparum malaria can be fatal. One negative rapid antigen test and one negative film set do not exclude malaria. Australian guidance (eTG and the laboratory recommendations) is to repeat thick and thin films every 12 to 24 hours until three sets are negative. A thickened gallbladder wall without stones, without a sonographic Murphy's sign and without duct dilatation is a common finding in acute hepatitis and needs no further biliary imaging. The diagnosis is already confirmed, so no further serology or tissue is needed.
why: A HIDA scan looks for acalculous or calculous cholecystitis, but gallbladder wall thickening without stones or ductal dilatation is an expected reactive finding in acute viral hepatitis.
MRCP looks for biliary obstruction, which is unlikely with a normal-calibre common bile duct and a hepatocellular rather than cholestatic pattern of liver tests.
Hepatitis A IgG shows past infection or immunity and adds nothing once IgM has already confirmed acute infection.
Liver biopsy is invasive and not needed when serology has confirmed acute hepatitis A and the INR shows preserved synthetic function.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has fever and 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound confirms calculous cholecystitis; common bile duct 5 mm. ALP 480 U/L, bilirubin 24 µmol/L.
items.explanation: A blocked cystic duct alone usually causes only mild LFT changes. An ALP more than 4 times the upper limit means a common bile duct stone is possible, even though the bilirubin is only slightly raised and the duct is not dilated, because partial obstruction often looks like this. This puts her at intermediate risk, so she needs non-invasive duct imaging with MRCP (or endoscopic ultrasound) before cholecystectomy.
why: ERCP carries a risk of pancreatitis and bleeding, so it is kept for a confirmed duct stone or cholangitis, and neither has been shown here.
Ultrasound has already confirmed cholecystitis, and a HIDA scan cannot reliably show stones in the common bile duct.
CT misses many bile duct stones and adds radiation without answering the question.
Repeat ultrasound sees the distal common bile duct poorly and is no better at finding a stone than the first scan.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has 6 weeks of burning epigastric pain waking him at night. He takes no medications and has no weight loss, vomiting or melaena. Haemoglobin is 146 g/L.
items.explanation: This young man has dyspepsia that sounds like a duodenal ulcer, takes no NSAIDs and has no ALARM features. eTG recommends a test-and-treat approach in this case: a non-invasive test for current H. pylori infection, either a urea breath test or a faecal antigen test, done when he has been off PPIs and antibiotics.
why: Gastroscopy is kept for patients with ALARM features, older patients with new symptoms, or symptoms that persist after test and treat, and he has none of these.
Serology stays positive after the infection has been cleared, so it cannot show current infection and is not recommended.
Ultrasound looks for gallstones, but burning nocturnal pain without colic or right upper quadrant features does not point to biliary disease.
Lipase is for acute pancreatitis, which would cause severe constant pain going through to the back, not weeks of intermittent burning nocturnal pain.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has full-thickness circumferential burns of the left forearm after a house fire. Six hours into resuscitation, his hand is cool and pale with no radial Doppler signal.
items.explanation: Full-thickness burn eschar is stiff and does not stretch. As the tissue swells during fluid resuscitation, a circumferential eschar acts like a tourniquet and cuts off blood flow to the hand. Loss of distal perfusion is a clinical diagnosis, and Australian burns guidelines (ANZBA EMSB) call for urgent escharotomy to release the eschar and restore circulation.
why: Fasciotomy is kept for compartment syndrome that persists after escharotomy, or for electrical or crush injury, so it is not the first step here.
Elevation helps reduce swelling but cannot release a constricting eschar once the pulse is lost.
Cutting back fluids risks under-resuscitation and shock; the fluid rate should be guided by urine output, not by limb swelling.
Imaging delays a decision that should be made at the bedside on clinical grounds, and the limb is at risk of irreversible ischaemia.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has two weeks of worsening thoracic back pain and new bilateral leg weakness. Reflexes are brisk in both legs.
items.explanation: New back pain, leg weakness and upper motor neuron signs in a patient with known cancer suggest malignant spinal cord compression. This needs an urgent whole spine MRI, ideally within 24 hours, along with high-dose dexamethasone. The whole spine is imaged because about a third of patients have compression at more than one level.
why: Plain X-rays cannot show the spinal cord or epidural disease and miss many metastases, so a normal film would not rule out compression.
A bone scan can show bone metastases but not compression of the cord or the epidural space, so it does not guide urgent treatment.
PSA reflects overall disease burden but cannot confirm or locate cord compression, and checking it would only delay definitive imaging.
CT shows less soft tissue and cord detail than MRI and is kept for patients who cannot have MRI; imaging only the thoracic spine would also miss lesions at other levels.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with diabetes has 40 minutes of central chest pain at rest despite aspirin, sublingual and intravenous GTN, and morphine. ECG shows no ST elevation; first troponin is normal.
items.explanation: Ongoing ischaemic pain that does not respond to nitrates and opioid makes this suspected NSTEACS very high risk under the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guideline, even with a normal ECG and a normal first troponin. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography within 2 hours, so cardiology should be contacted now.
why: Thrombolysis is only for STEMI and does not help in non-ST-elevation ACS.
Serial troponins are still needed, but waiting for them delays angiography, which very high-risk features require now.
CT coronary angiography is for low to intermediate risk stable patients, not for ongoing ischaemia, and it cannot open a blocked artery.
Stress testing is unsafe during ongoing pain and is only for low-risk patients once ACS has been ruled out.

items.stem: An 82-year-old man from a nursing home has 3 days of abdominal distension and absolute constipation. He is afebrile without peritonism. Abdominal X-ray shows a coffee-bean sign arising from the pelvis.
items.explanation: This is a sigmoid volvulus with no signs of ischaemia or perforation. First-line treatment is flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression with a flatus tube, then sigmoid colectomy during the same admission if the patient is fit, because the volvulus often comes back.
why: Emergency surgery is for peritonitis, perforation, ischaemic mucosa seen at endoscopy, or failed decompression, and none of these is present.
Neostigmine treats acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome), not a mechanical twist of the sigmoid colon.
A contrast enema can confirm the diagnosis (bird's-beak sign), but the X-ray already shows it, and an enema does not reliably decompress the bowel.
Colonic stents are used for malignant large bowel obstruction, not for untwisting a volvulus.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever and new confusion. After IV fluids and antibiotics, BP is 94/60 mmHg. Ultrasound: dilated common bile duct, distal stone.
items.explanation: Jaundice, pain, fever, confusion and hypotension make up Reynolds' pentad. This is severe acute cholangitis from an obstructing common bile duct stone. Once sepsis resuscitation and IV antibiotics have started, he needs urgent biliary drainage by ERCP for source control, with cholecystectomy planned after he recovers.
why: Emergency cholecystectomy in a septic, unstable patient does not clear the duct stone; it is done after he has recovered.
MRCP only images the duct, which ultrasound has already shown is blocked, and it would delay drainage.
Cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the obstructed common bile duct, so it is used for high-risk acute cholecystitis.
Antibiotics alone leave the duct obstructed, and organ dysfunction in severe cholangitis means he needs urgent drainage.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man comes to his general practitioner because of episodes of a racing, irregular heartbeat. Over the past 6 weeks he has had four episodes. Each started suddenly at rest, lasted 1 to 3 hours and stopped on its own. He has had no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and takes perindopril and metformin. He drinks about four standard drinks of alcohol a day and has never smoked. He arrived during an episode. A 12-lead ECG then showed an irregularly irregular, narrow-complex rhythm at 104/min with no P waves. Two hours later his pulse is 74/min and regular, blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg and SpO2 is 98% on room air. Heart sounds are normal with no murmurs. Haemoglobin is 142 g/L, creatinine 86 µmol/L (eGFR 79 mL/min/1.73 m^2), potassium 4.3 mmol/L and TSH 1.8 mIU/L. A repeat ECG shows sinus rhythm.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to start today?
items.explanation: This man has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: sudden irregular palpitations that stop on their own, an ECG during an episode showing AF, and sinus rhythm afterwards. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 3 (age 65 to 74, hypertension, diabetes). Stroke risk in paroxysmal AF is about the same as in persistent AF, so the score, not the pattern of episodes, decides anticoagulation. The 2018 NHFA/CSANZ Australian AF guidelines and eTG recommend oral anticoagulation for a CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 or more. They prefer a DOAC such as apixaban over warfarin in non-valvular AF because it causes less intracranial bleeding and needs no INR monitoring. items.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner on the afternoon after his first half marathon (21 km). His longest previous run was 10 km, three weeks ago. Over the final 6 km he became gradually more short of breath, slowed to a walk, and felt back to normal within 15 minutes of finishing. He had no chest pain, palpitations, light-headedness, syncope, wheeze, cough, throat tightness or haemoptysis. He has no history of asthma or atopy, and no recent surgery, travel or immobilisation. He takes no medicines and does not smoke. No family member has died suddenly of a cardiac cause. He is 183 cm tall and weighs 75 kg. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 64/min and regular, respirations 14/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, and SpO2 99% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable, with no calf swelling or tenderness. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with no abnormalities. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.85 (LLN 0.72) and FEV1 101% predicted, with a change of +100 mL (2%) after salbutamol.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Salbutamol inhaler, two puffs 15 minutes before each run
Mannitol bronchial provocation test in a respiratory laboratory

Transthoracic echocardiogram to look for cardiomyopathy
Reassurance, a slower mileage build-up and return precautions

The right management is to explain this and reassure him, advise a gradual increase in distance, and safety-net: he should return urgently if he gets chest pain, syncope, palpitations, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or wheeze, or if the breathlessness keeps happening at distances he is used to. He does not need more tests or treatment. He is PERC negative with a low pretest probability, so the eTG advises no D-dimer. A bronchial provocation test is kept for people whose symptoms suggest exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

Wrong: provocation testing is used when symptoms suggest exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, which he does not have, so it would not change management.
Wrong: he has a low pretest probability and meets every PERC criterion, so a D-dimer is not indicated and could give a false positive that leads to unnecessary CTPA.
Wrong: he has no exertional chest pain, syncope, palpitations, murmur, family history of sudden death or ECG abnormality, so echocardiography is not indicated.

items.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has had a discharging left ear for 8 weeks. Otoscopy shows pus and a central tympanic membrane perforation. He is afebrile.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman, a professional violinist, is consenting to elective carpal tunnel release. She repeatedly asks whether surgery could affect her playing. The quoted nerve injury risk is below 1%.
items.ask: Which risk is most important to disclose?
items.explanation: Under Rogers v Whitaker (1992), a doctor must disclose material risks. A risk is material if a reasonable person would care about it, or if the doctor knows or should know that this particular patient would. Nerve injury is rare, but it could end this patient's career, and her questions show she cares about it, so it must be disclosed whatever its frequency.
why: Infection is more common and should be mentioned, but it is usually minor and treatable, and it does not threaten what she has said matters most.

Systemic reactions to local anaesthetic are very rare and do not relate to her stated concern about hand function.
DVT after a short upper-limb procedure under local anaesthetic is very unlikely and is not what she is worried about.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 6 months of numbness and intermittent shooting pain in both feet. He feels unsteady when he walks to the bathroom at night. He has no back pain and no bladder or bowel symptoms. He has had type 2 diabetes for 8 years and has taken metformin 1 g twice daily the whole time, along with ramipril. He drinks two standard drinks a week and eats a mixed diet. His blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Pinprick and 10 g monofilament sensation are reduced symmetrically to the mid-shins. Vibration sense is absent at both great toes. Ankle reflexes are absent, knee reflexes are normal and plantar responses are flexor. Power and tone are normal. Romberg test is positive. Pedal pulses are palpable. Investigations: HbA1c 8.4% (target 7.0% or less), haemoglobin 141 g/L, MCV 92 fL (80 to 100), eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73 m2 and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5 to 4.0).
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Nerve conduction studies of the legs
items.explanation: This man has a typical distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy. The loss is length-dependent and stocking-shaped, he has lost protective sensation and vibration sense, his ankle reflexes are absent while his knee reflexes are kept, and he has sensory ataxia. This fits poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. Before calling it diabetic neuropathy, the treatable mimics need to be excluded. His TSH and eGFR are normal and he drinks little, so the main mimic left is vitamin B12 deficiency. Metformin reduces B12 absorption, and he has taken it for 8 years. A normal MCV does not exclude B12 deficiency, because neuropathy can come before anaemia or macrocytosis. Australian guidance (eTG Diabetes and the RACGP type 2 diabetes handbook) recommends checking B12 in people on long-term metformin, especially when neuropathy appears. Diabetic neuropathy is a clinical diagnosis, so nerve conduction studies, imaging, CSF analysis and biopsy are only needed for atypical features. These include asymmetry, rapid progression, marked weakness, early involvement of the hands, or upper motor neuron or sphincter signs.

Wrong: he has no back pain, sphincter symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, upper motor neuron signs or dermatomal pattern, so imaging the spine is not indicated.

Wrong: CSF protein is used when chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is suspected, which presents with proximal and distal weakness and loss of all reflexes, not a purely distal sensory picture.
Wrong: nerve biopsy is invasive and is kept for suspected vasculitic or infiltrative neuropathy, which would present with asymmetric or rapidly progressive deficits.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter with 3 days of worsening breathlessness and green sputum. She has COPD and smokes 30 cigarettes a day (about 55 pack-years). Her medicines are tiotropium and budesonide-formoterol inhalers. At triage her SpO2 was 84% on room air. She was put on 15 L/min oxygen through a reservoir bag device and given nebulised salbutamol driven by 8 L/min wall oxygen. Forty minutes later she is drowsy but opens her eyes to voice and obeys commands. She has a flapping tremor. Temperature 37.9 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 150/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 99%. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. Arterial blood gas on her current oxygen: pH 7.27 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 78 mmHg (35 to 45), PaO2 165 mmHg, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L (22 to 26). A gas taken at a clinic visit 4 months ago showed PaCO2 54 mmHg with a normal pH.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Switch to a 28% Venturi device aiming for saturations of 88 to 92%
Remove all supplemental oxygen at once
Start bilevel non-invasive ventilation at the current oxygen flow rate
Arrange rapid sequence intubation and mechanical ventilation
items.explanation: This woman is a known chronic CO2 retainer: her earlier PaCO2 was 54 mmHg with a normal pH, and her bicarbonate is raised. She was given uncontrolled high-flow oxygen and an oxygen-driven nebuliser. She now has oxygen-induced hypercapnic acidosis. The clues are drowsiness, a flapping tremor, a falling respiratory rate, SpO2 99% with a PaO2 of 165 mmHg, and an acute rise in PaCO2 with a pH of 7.27. Excess oxygen raises PaCO2 because it worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch (it reverses hypoxic vasoconstriction), adds the Haldane effect and reduces respiratory drive. The TSANZ oxygen guideline and COPD-X say oxygen in COPD should be controlled with a target SpO2 of 88 to 92%, and nebulisers should be driven by air. When oxygen-induced hypercapnia happens, step oxygen down to that target with a Venturi device. Do not stop it abruptly. Then repeat the blood gas in 30 to 60 minutes. Non-invasive ventilation is for acidosis that persists despite optimal treatment, and that includes controlled oxygen.
why: Wrong: stopping oxygen abruptly causes rebound hypoxaemia that can be severe and fatal, because PaO2 falls faster than the stored CO2 can be cleared, so oxygen should be stepped down, not removed.
Wrong: NIV is for hypercapnic acidosis that persists despite optimal treatment, and running it at the same excessive oxygen flow would leave the cause of the acidosis in place.
Wrong: she obeys commands and has a reversible, iatrogenic cause, so intubation is not yet needed and should be kept for failure of controlled oxygen and NIV.
Wrong: this is a respiratory acidosis, and bicarbonate does not treat the cause and can increase CO2 production, so it has no role here.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 18 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain that began after a takeaway dinner. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and drinks alcohol occasionally. Her temperature is 38.4 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg and respiratory rate 18/min. She is not jaundiced and is alert. Her right upper quadrant is tender, and Murphy's sign is positive. Blood tests show: white cell count 14.9 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP 128 mg/L (<5), total bilirubin 15 µmol/L (<20), ALP 131 U/L (30–110), GGT 52 U/L (<38), ALT 44 U/L (<35), lipase 40 U/L (<60) and serum beta-hCG <2 IU/L. Hepatocellular injury, suggesting a superimposed acute viral hepatitis

items.explanation: She has acute calculous cholecystitis. With a normal bilirubin, a normal duct calibre and no stone seen, her risk of a common bile duct stone is low. She does not need a preoperative MRCP or ERCP and can go to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with IV antibiotics as eTG recommends. A raised bilirubin, a dilated duct or a duct stone would change this. With fever, they would point to cholangitis. Option A is wrong because a blocked duct would normally raise the bilirubin and widen the duct, and she has neither. Option B is wrong because the transaminases are barely raised and the pattern is mildly cholestatic, not the large ALT rise of acute hepatitis. Option D is wrong because cholangitis needs signs of a blocked duct (jaundice or a raised bilirubin, a dilated duct) as well as fever, and she has none. Acute viral hepatitis causes a large ALT rise, often in the hundreds or thousands, but her ALT is only 44 U/L with a mildly cholestatic pattern, and the ultrasound explains her symptoms.
Cholangitis needs fever plus evidence of a blocked duct, such as jaundice, a raised bilirubin or a dilated duct, and she has none of these, so urgent decompression is not needed.
A small GGT rise alongside a raised ALP fits reactive cholestasis, and she rarely drinks, so alcohol does not explain these results.

items.explanation: She has early, seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis with poor prognostic features, so she needs a DMARD started now to prevent more joint damage. The most important risk in her case is the drug harming a pregnancy, because she is trying to conceive and will not use contraception. Under eTG and Australian Rheumatology Association guidance, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are the conventional synthetic DMARDs that can be used before conception and through pregnancy. Sulfasalazine is started at a low dose and increased to 1 g twice daily. It is a folate antagonist, so she should also take high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) before conception. It can be combined with hydroxychloroquine and short-term low-dose prednisolone if needed. She should plan her pregnancy with the rheumatologist and stop naproxen while trying to conceive. Leflunomide and methotrexate are teratogenic and need reliable contraception. Mycophenolate and tofacitinib are also unsuitable.
why: Leflunomide is teratogenic and its active metabolite stays in the body for up to 2 years, so a woman trying to conceive would need a washout with cholestyramine; it is contraindicated for her.

Methotrexate is usually the first-line DMARD, but it is teratogenic and abortifacient, so it needs reliable contraception and must be stopped before conception; it is contraindicated while she is actively trying to conceive.
Mycophenolate is a strong teratogen that causes miscarriage and malformations, and it is not a standard DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis.
Tofacitinib is a JAK inhibitor that should be avoided around conception and in pregnancy, and in Australia it is reserved for disease that has not responded to conventional synthetic DMARDs.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman sees her general practitioner with 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. She is not breathless and has no chest pain. She has no past medical history, takes no medicines or supplements, and has a contraceptive implant. Temperature is 37.0 °C, pulse 110/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She is alert and has a fine tremor, warm moist hands, and bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis, with normal visual acuity, colour vision and eye movements. There is a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with a bruit. There are no signs of heart failure. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 110/min with narrow QRS complexes. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 48 pmol/L (10–20), free T3 18.5 pmol/L (3.5–6.5) and TSH receptor antibodies 12.4 IU/L (<1.8). Full blood count, liver function tests and serum beta-hCG are normal.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: She has Graves' disease, shown by suppressed TSH, high free T4 and T3, strongly positive TRAb, a diffuse goitre with a bruit and orbitopathy. It is complicated by thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation. She is haemodynamically stable, afebrile and alert, with no heart failure, so she does not have thyroid storm and can be managed as an outpatient. eTG recommends a non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol to control the heart rate and adrenergic symptoms. It also recommends a thionamide, with carbimazole first-line outside the first trimester, to make her euthyroid. Baseline FBC and LFTs are normal and she is not pregnant. Thyrotoxic AF usually reverts to sinus rhythm once she is euthyroid. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so anticoagulation is not indicated. She must be told to stop carbimazole and have a same-day FBC if she gets a sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers. Amiodarone is wrong because its iodine load worsens thyrotoxicosis, and she does not need anticoagulation. Digoxin works poorly in a hyperadrenergic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester or thyroid storm because it can damage the liver. Radioiodine is not first-line here and can worsen her active orbitopathy. Cardioversion while she is still thyrotoxic usually fails, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid.
why: Amiodarone's iodine load can worsen thyrotoxicosis, and with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 0 she does not need anticoagulation.
Digoxin controls the rate poorly in a hyperadrenergic thyrotoxic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester of pregnancy or thyroid storm because it can cause severe liver injury.
Radioiodine is not first-line treatment for a new, uncontrolled presentation and can worsen her active Graves' orbitopathy, especially before she is euthyroid.
Cardioversion in a patient who is still thyrotoxic often fails and the AF tends to come back, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid, by which time the AF usually reverts on its own.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man, a retired plumber exposed to asbestos, has months of dry cough and breathlessness. Room-air SpO2 is 95% at rest, 90% after a 50 m walk, recovering within minutes.
items.ask: Best interpretation of these oximetry readings?
items.explanation: His SpO2 is normal at rest, then falls by 5 points (to 90%) after only 50 m and recovers when he rests. That is exertional desaturation, an objective sign of significant lung disease that matches his breathlessness. In an asbestos-exposed man it adds weight to urgent imaging and specialist referral.
why: An SpO2 of 95% at rest on room air is normal, so he is not hypoxaemic at rest.
Type 2 respiratory failure means hypercapnia, which can only be shown on a blood gas, and a brief fall in SpO2 on exertion does not show it.
A reading that falls in a repeatable way with exertion and recovers at rest suggests a physiological change rather than a faulty probe.
Healthy older adults keep their saturation steady on a short, gentle walk, so a drop to 90% after 50 m is abnormal.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 10 days of worsening breathlessness. It has been severe since overnight, and she has orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Six weeks ago she had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent. Since then she has been taking over-the-counter naproxen for knee pain. Her pulse is 110/min and regular, blood pressure 194/102 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 87% on room air. She has a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound and bilateral basal crackles. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior Q waves, unchanged from her discharge ECG. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacification and small effusions. NT-proBNP is 7900 ng/L (age-adjusted rule-in level above 900 ng/L). High-sensitivity troponin I is 38 ng/L, then 37 ng/L at 3 hours (female 99th percentile 16 ng/L). Creatinine is 142 µmol/L. After CPAP, glyceryl trinitrate and intravenous furosemide, she is comfortable on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal prongs.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This woman has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. She has orthopnoea, PND, a raised JVP, an S3, crackles, alveolar oedema with effusions on X-ray and a very high NT-proBNP. The likely cause is ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction after her recent anterior MI, made worse by NSAID-related fluid retention and hypertension. Her two troponin values are stable and barely raised, and her ECG has not changed, so this is chronic myocardial injury rather than a new infarct. The 2018 National Heart Foundation and CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. Echo confirms the diagnosis and measures the LVEF, which decides between HFrEF and HFpEF and therefore which survival-improving treatments she should get. Echo also looks for mechanical complications of the recent MI (mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect, aneurysm, left ventricular thrombus), regional wall motion problems and valve disease. It is quick, done at the bedside and needs no contrast or radiation.
why: Incorrect: orthopnoea, PND, an S3, alveolar oedema and an NT-proBNP of 7900 explain her hypoxia, so pulmonary embolism is unlikely and iodinated contrast with a creatinine of 142 µmol/L brings risk for no gain.
Incorrect: her troponin is flat with no new ECG change, so there is no acute coronary syndrome needing urgent angiography, and the contrast load would add to her kidney injury.
Incorrect: cardiac MRI is a second-line test for when echo images are poor or the cause is unclear, not the first test for ventricular function in an acutely unwell patient.
Incorrect: a V/Q scan tests for pulmonary embolism, which the clinical picture does not suggest, and alveolar oedema and effusions make the scan hard to interpret.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman with BMI 43 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes has 10 months of irregular, heavy bleeding. Pipelle biopsy shows endometrial hyperplasia without atypia.
items.ask: Main mechanism linking her obesity to this?
items.explanation: Adipose tissue converts androgens (mainly androstenedione) into oestrone. With anovulation there is no progesterone to oppose it, so the endometrium is driven to hyperplasia and cancer. Hyperinsulinaemia adds to the risk by lowering SHBG and raising IGF-1, so counsel her that losing weight and taking a progestogen reduce her risk.
why: Obesity and hyperinsulinaemia lower SHBG rather than raise it, which leaves more free oestrogen.
Obesity-related anovulation means there is no luteal progesterone, and that lack is what leaves the oestrogen unopposed.
Obesity tends to raise androgen levels, which gives more substrate for aromatisation.
Obesity and type 2 diabetes cause hyperinsulinaemia, and the raised insulin and IGF-1 promote endometrial growth.

items.stem: An 86-year-old woman trips at home and strikes her forehead. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. She is alert, GCS 15, with a small forehead haematoma and no neurological deficit.
items.explanation: Older adults taking anticoagulants who have a head injury are at high risk of intracranial haemorrhage, even when GCS is 15 and the neurological exam is normal. Australian adult head injury guidelines, such as NSW Health's, call for a non-contrast CT brain in this situation. Reversal is used only if a bleed is confirmed.
why: Skull X-ray cannot rule out intracranial haemorrhage and has no role in current head injury assessment.
Anticoagulant reversal is for a confirmed significant bleed, not a head injury that has not yet been imaged.
Sending her home without imaging misses a delayed or hidden intracranial haemorrhage, which is more likely with anticoagulation.
Watching her without imaging is not enough, because anticoagulated older patients can bleed without early clinical signs.
